children.title: Scheduling Complexity-Certificate Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Complexity classification and reusable structural principles supporting exact or approximate scheduling.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Complexity Hierarchy; Complexity Classification of Scheduling Problems

children.title: Efficient Scheduling Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Polynomial and pseudopolynomial families arising from restricted environments, structures, or objectives.

children.title: Polynomial Scheduling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Restricted scheduling families admitting polynomial-time solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Scheduling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity classification for deterministic scheduling decision problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance be encoded by a binary string \(x\), with length \(L=|x|\), and let \(D(x)\) denote its scheduling decision predicate. The regime is polynomially solvable if there exist a deterministic algorithm and constants \(c,k>0\) such that, for every valid instance \(x\), the algorithm returns \(D(x)\) after at most \(cL^k\) elementary bit operations. Thus the bound is polynomial in the complete binary input length, including the logarithmic encoding lengths of all integer processing times, capacities, deadlines, and costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scheduling regime is polynomial when its decision problem is solvable in time polynomial in the full binary input length.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a finite binary encoding of a valid scheduling instance.
Arithmetic costs are measured in elementary bit operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(x)\le c|x|^k\) for fixed constants \(c,k>0\).

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

children.title: Pseudopolynomial Scheduling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Scheduling families whose solvability depends polynomially on numeric magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudopolynomial Scheduling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic-magnitude complexity for integer-valued scheduling instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) encode a scheduling instance with combinatorial size \(n\) and nonnegative integer data \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\), and put \(U=\max_i a_i\). An exact algorithm is pseudopolynomial if its running time is bounded by a polynomial \(q(n,m,U)\), although the binary input length contains only \(O(\sum_i\log(1+a_i))\) bits for these numbers. Such a bound need not be polynomial in binary input length because \(U\) may be exponential in \(\log U\); it becomes polynomial when the numeric data are unary encoded or polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudopolynomial scheduling algorithm is polynomial in combinatorial size and numeric values, but not necessarily in their binary encoding lengths.
assumptions_latex: All magnitude-sensitive scheduling data are nonnegative integers.
The algorithm is exact and uses the standard binary input encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(x)\le q(n,m,U)\), which is polynomial under unary encoding or when \(U\le n^{O(1)}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pseudopolynomial distinction is mathematically plausible and fits the terminal container, but no inspectable source supports the stated definition and its unary-encoding and polynomial-magnitude consequences.

children.title: Structural Sources of Tractability
children.top_down_role: Restrictions on environments, precedence, processing times, or objectives that simplify scheduling.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Sources of Tractability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A parameterized criterion converting structural restrictions into exact polynomial algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a scheduling family parameterized by a structural quantity \(w\), such as the number of machines, precedence width, treewidth of a constraint graph, or number of job types. If an exact algorithm has running time \(f(w)L^k\), where \(L\) is binary input length, \(k\) is constant, and \(f\) is independent of \(L\), then every subfamily satisfying \(w\le w_0\) for a fixed constant \(w_0\) is polynomially solvable. Structural tractability therefore follows from a proved parameterized bound together with a fixed bound on the relevant structural parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed structural parameter yields polynomial solvability whenever an exact algorithm runs in parameter-dependent polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is exact and has running time \(f(w)L^k\).
The restricted family satisfies \(w\le w_0\) for a constant \(w_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(L)\le f(w_0)L^k=O(L^k)\) on the restricted family.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional parameterized-time argument is correct and the principle kind fits the container, but the record has no source for its scheduling and parameterized-complexity formulation.

children.title: Numeric-Magnitude Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes caused by encoding length or bounded numeric parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Magnitude Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes dependence on numeric values from dependence on their encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be the largest nonnegative integer appearing in a scheduling instance and let \(L\) be its binary encoding length. A running-time bound polynomial in \(U\) is magnitude-sensitive because the encoding contributes only \(O(\log(1+U))\) bits. Consequently, a bound \(T\le q(n,U)\) can be exponential as a function of \(L\). If all numeric values satisfy \(U\le n^c\) for a fixed \(c\), the same bound becomes polynomial in \(n\) and hence in the total input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial dependence on an integer value may be exponential in its bit length, but polynomially bounded values remove that gap.
assumptions_latex: Numeric scheduling data are nonnegative integers encoded in binary.
\(q\) is a fixed polynomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial dependence on \(U\) does not imply polynomial bit complexity unless \(U\) is polynomially bounded or unary encoded.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The value-versus-bit-length distinction is precise and appropriate as a property, but the nontrivial complexity claims have no cited source.

children.title: Scheduling Hardness Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Hardness regimes distinguishing numeric from persistent combinatorial difficulty.

children.title: Weak Scheduling Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness tied to numeric magnitudes or compact numeric encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Scheduling Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-versus-unary definition of weak NP-hardness for numeric scheduling families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scheduling decision problem \(D\) with integer data is weakly NP-hard if \(D\) is NP-hard under binary encoding, while the restriction \(D_{\mathrm{unary}}\), obtained by unary encoding or polynomially bounding every numeric datum, is solvable in polynomial time. Equivalently for the intended classification, the known hardness can disappear when numeric magnitudes are bounded, leaving open or permitting a pseudopolynomial exact algorithm. Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\), when established separately, upgrades the corresponding binary-encoded decision problem from weakly NP-hard to weakly NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak scheduling hardness depends on binary-encoded numeric magnitudes and disappears under unary encoding or polynomial magnitude bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a scheduling decision problem with nonnegative integer data.
Binary and unary versions preserve the same feasibility and objective-threshold semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is NP-hard in binary encoding and \(D_{\mathrm{unary}}\in\mathrm{P}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An authoritative complexity source is required because definitions of weak NP-hardness vary, and the asserted equivalence among unary encoding, polynomial magnitude bounds, and disappearance of hardness requires explicit qualification.

children.title: Strong Scheduling Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness persisting under polynomially bounded numeric data.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Scheduling Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong NP-hardness under polynomially bounded numeric scheduling data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scheduling decision problem \(D\) with integer data is strongly NP-hard if there exists a polynomial \(p\) such that the restriction of \(D\) to instances whose every numeric datum is at most \(p(n)\) remains NP-hard, where \(n\) is the combinatorial instance size. Equivalently, NP-hardness persists under unary encoding of the numeric data. Unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), a strongly NP-hard problem admits no pseudopolynomial exact algorithm, because such an algorithm would run in polynomial time on the polynomially bounded hard restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong scheduling hardness persists even when all numeric data are polynomially bounded or encoded in unary.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a scheduling decision problem with integer data.
The restricted instances retain polynomial-size encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a polynomial \(p\) for which \(D\) restricted by \(U\le p(n)\) is NP-hard.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation matches the intended strong-hardness container, but its equivalence with unary-encoded hardness and its pseudopolynomial-algorithm consequence require an authoritative source and stated encoding conventions.

children.title: Numeric Versus Combinatorial Hardness
children.top_down_role: The boundary between magnitude-driven difficulty and persistent structural difficulty.

knowledge_statements.title: Numeric Versus Combinatorial Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic separation of magnitude-driven and structure-driven scheduling hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scheduling decision family with combinatorial size \(n\) and largest numeric datum \(U\), compare the unrestricted problem with the restriction \(U\le n^c\) for a fixed constant \(c\). If NP-hardness disappears and a polynomial algorithm applies on every such bounded-magnitude restriction, the obstruction is numeric and is consistent with weak hardness. If NP-hardness persists for some polynomial bound on \(U\), the obstruction is combinatorial and establishes strong hardness. This comparison classifies the hardness mechanism, not merely the encoding convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound numeric magnitudes: disappearing hardness indicates a numeric source, while persisting NP-hardness indicates a combinatorial source.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling family has explicitly identified integer data.
The bounded-magnitude restriction preserves the combinatorial constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Persistence of NP-hardness under \(U\le n^{O(1)}\) separates combinatorial hardness from magnitude-dependent hardness.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagnostic is consistent with the weak-versus-strong hardness distinction, but no source supports the claimed classification of numeric and combinatorial hardness mechanisms.

children.title: Restricted-Regime Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness that survives limitations on machines, precedences, durations, or objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Regime Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for hardness surviving an explicitly defined scheduling restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be a scheduling decision problem and let \(R\) be a polynomial-time recognizable predicate defining a restricted instance class. Hardness in the restricted regime holds when there is a polynomial-time many-one reduction \(f\) from an NP-hard language \(H\) such that, for every input \(y\), the instance \(f(y)\) satisfies \(R\) and \(y\in H\) if and only if \(f(y)\in D\). The reduction must preserve every advertised restriction, such as a fixed machine count, bounded processing times, or a specified precedence topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted-regime hardness requires a polynomial reduction whose output always satisfies every stated scheduling restriction.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
\(R\) is polynomial-time recognizable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\le_m^p D|_R\), so the restricted problem \(D|_R\) is NP-hard.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction condition is mathematically precise and fits the restricted-regime container, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

children.title: Schedule-Transformation Dominance Calculus
children.top_down_role: Order and schedule transformations that reduce the candidate space.

children.title: Schedule Dominance Principles
children.top_down_role: Structural comparisons that remove inferior schedules or partial schedules.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Dominance Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-preserving feasibility transformations that justify restricting the schedule search space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the feasible schedules of an instance, let \(F:S\to\mathbb{R}\) be minimized, and let \(T:S\to S\) be a computable transformation satisfying \(F(T(s))\le F(s)\) for every \(s\in S\). Then the image \(T(S)\) is a dominant schedule class: for every feasible schedule there is a schedule in \(T(S)\) with no larger objective value. Consequently, if an optimum exists, at least one optimum lies in \(T(S)\), so search may be restricted to that image without changing the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible transformation that never worsens the objective defines a dominant class containing an optimal schedule.
assumptions_latex: \(S\ne\varnothing\), and the minimum of \(F\) over \(S\) is attained.
\(T(s)\in S\) and \(F(T(s))\le F(s)\) for every \(s\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{s\in S}F(s)=\min_{s\in T(S)}F(s)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transformation argument correctly defines a dominant schedule class and fits a principle container, but it lacks a scheduling-dominance source.

children.title: Adjacent Interchange Principles
children.top_down_role: Local sequence transformations used to compare neighboring job orders.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjacent Interchange Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local pairwise-exchange criterion for deriving an optimal job order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite job set with a strict total preferred order \(\prec\). Consider a feasible sequence in which adjacent jobs \(j,i\), with \(i\prec j\), start after a common prefix completed at time \(t\). Let \(C_{ij}(t)\) and \(C_{ji}(t)\) include every objective contribution changed by ordering the pair as \(i,j\) or \(j,i\), respectively. If every such adjacent inversion is feasibly swappable and \(C_{ij}(t)\le C_{ji}(t)\) for every reachable \(t\), then repeatedly swapping adjacent inversions does not worsen the objective and terminates at the unique sequence ordered by \(\prec\). Applied to an optimal sequence, these swaps produce an optimal sequence respecting \(\prec\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every adjacent inversion of a strict total job order can be feasibly swapped without worsening the complete objective, an optimal sequence exists that respects that order.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and \(\prec\) is a strict total order on \(J\).
Every adjacent \(\prec\)-inversion is feasibly swappable.
\(C_{ij}(t)\) and \(C_{ji}(t)\) account for every objective term changed by the swap.
An optimal feasible sequence exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an optimal feasible sequence containing no inversion of \(\prec\).

notation.meaning: strict total preferred order on the jobs
completion time of the common prefix
complete affected cost when job i precedes job j

children.title: Global Interchange Principles
children.top_down_role: Nonlocal schedule transformations preserving feasibility while improving structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Interchange Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension of valid local exchanges to globally ordered optimal schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\) be a finite job set with a strict total preferred order \(\prec\), and let \(F\) be an objective to be minimized over feasible job sequences. Suppose every feasible sequence containing an adjacent inversion \(j,i\), with \(i\prec j\), admits the swap to \(i,j\) while preserving feasibility and not increasing \(F\). Each such swap strictly decreases the finite inversion count relative to \(\prec\), so repeated swaps terminate at the sequence ordered by \(\prec\). Starting from an optimal feasible sequence, the process therefore produces an optimal feasible sequence respecting \(\prec\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible nonworsening swaps of every adjacent inversion of a strict total order produce an optimal schedule respecting that global order.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is finite and \(\prec\) is a strict total order on \(J\).
Every adjacent \(\prec\)-inversion is feasibly swappable without increasing \(F\).
An optimal feasible sequence exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some optimal feasible sequence orders all jobs according to \(\prec\).

children.title: Dominance Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which dominance or interchange arguments cease to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Validity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which pairwise schedule dominance does not extend to the full model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An interchange rule derived from \(C_{ij}(t)\le C_{ji}(t)\) is valid only when the exchange preserves feasibility and the computed difference includes every objective term changed by the swap. The inference can fail when jobs have release dates, sequence-dependent setup times, machine eligibility, precedence constraints, resource coupling, or nonseparable costs: swapping \(j,i\) may become infeasible or may alter downstream completion times and costs omitted from \(C_{ij}(t)-C_{ji}(t)\). Therefore local pairwise improvement alone does not certify global dominance outside the assumptions used to derive it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interchange dominance fails when swaps violate constraints or alter downstream costs omitted from the pairwise comparison.
assumptions_latex: The proposed rule compares two adjacent job orders.
The surrounding scheduling model may contain coupling constraints or nonseparable costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without feasibility preservation and complete cost accounting, \(C_{ij}(t)\le C_{ji}(t)\) does not imply global dominance.

notation.meaning: cost attributed to ordering job \(i\) before job \(j\)
state or time preceding the exchanged pair

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly identifies feasibility preservation and complete cost accounting as validity boundaries and uses the appropriate failure-boundary kind. The listed failure mechanisms and general conclusion nevertheless require an inspectable source.

children.title: Scheduling Bound-Relaxation Family
children.top_down_role: Workload, precedence, machine, Lagrangian, linear-programming, and surrogate bounds.

children.title: Workload Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds derived from aggregate processing demand and available capacity.

assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) jobs with processing times \(p_j\ge 0\) on \(m\ge 1\) identical parallel machines.
Each job is processed by exactly one machine, without simultaneous processing on multiple machines.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\max}\ge \max\{\max_j p_j,\,m^{-1}\sum_j p_j\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conservation of total machine processing capacity gives the workload bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identical-parallel-machine makespan bound, without release-time or precedence strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every feasible schedule, each job must receive \(p_j\) units of processing, so its completion requires at least \(\max_j p_j\) time. Moreover, the \(m\) machines can supply at most \(mC_{\max}\) units of processing by the makespan. Hence \[ C_{\max}\ge \max\!\left\{\max_{1\le j\le n}p_j,\;\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}p_j\right\}. \] If processing times and start times are integral, the workload term may be rounded up to \(\left\lceil \sum_jp_j/m\right\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A schedule cannot finish before its longest job or before enough time has elapsed for all machines collectively to process the total workload.
knowledge_statements.title: Workload Lower Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower bound is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but no inspectable scheduling source is cited. The current statement also contains a derivation, which should be removed when sourced.

children.title: Precedence Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds derived from chains, paths, or precedence-induced timing limits.

assumptions_latex: The precedence relation is an acyclic directed graph \(G=(J,E)\).
Every job \(j\in J\) has processing time \(p_j\ge 0\), and \((i,j)\in E\) requires job \(i\) to finish before job \(j\) starts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\max}\ge \max_{P}\sum_{j\in P}p_j\), where \(P\) ranges over directed paths of \(G\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: jobs on every precedence path must execute sequentially
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path lower bound for deterministic makespan scheduling on an acyclic precedence graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any directed path \(P=(j_1,\ldots,j_k)\) in \(G\), precedence feasibility implies that the jobs of \(P\) execute in their path order and cannot overlap one another. Consequently, every feasible schedule satisfies \[ C_{\max}\ge L_{\mathrm{prec}}:=\max_{P\text{ directed path in }G}\sum_{j\in P}p_j. \] The value \(L_{\mathrm{prec}}\) is the critical-path length and remains a valid lower bound regardless of the number of available machines.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every precedence path must be processed sequentially, so the longest path's total processing time is a lower bound on makespan.
knowledge_statements.title: Precedence Lower Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The critical-path bound is precise and locally appropriate, but it lacks a cited scheduling source and includes proof-style justification.

children.title: Machine-Based Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Bounds obtained by simplifying machine eligibility or interaction.

knowledge_statements.title: Machine-Based Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional assignment and machine-load relaxation for unrelated-parallel-machine makespan scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\{(i,j):p_{ij}<\infty\}\). The fractional machine-load relaxation is \[T_{\mathrm{ML}}:=\min\left\{T:\sum_{i:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}=1\ \forall j,\ \sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}p_{ij}x_{ij}\le T\ \forall i,\ x_{ij}\ge0\ \forall(i,j)\in E\right\}.\] Its optimum is a lower bound on the optimal nonpreemptive makespan: \(T_{\mathrm{ML}}\le C_{\max}^{\star}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing fractional job assignments while retaining machine-load constraints gives a relaxation whose optimum lower-bounds the optimal nonpreemptive makespan.
assumptions_latex: Job \(j\) requires time \(p_{ij}\in(0,\infty]\) if assigned to machine \(i\), with \(p_{ij}=\infty\) denoting an ineligible assignment.
The objective is to minimize makespan on unrelated parallel machines.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fractional machine-load optimum \(T_{\mathrm{ML}}\) satisfies \(T_{\mathrm{ML}}\le C_{\max}^{\star}\).

notation.meaning: Fraction of job j assigned to machine i in the relaxation

review_flags: scheduling specialization inferred from general LP-relaxation theory

children.title: Lagrangian Scheduling Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxations based on penalized coupling constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Scheduling Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak Lagrangian duality for minimization scheduling models with relaxed inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_{k=1}^{q}\lambda_k g_k(x),\qquad \theta(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}L(x,\lambda).\] For every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^q\), weak Lagrangian duality gives \(\theta(\lambda)\le z^{\star}\). Consequently, \[d^{\star}:=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^q}\theta(\lambda)\le z^{\star}.\] Equality is not asserted for a discrete scheduling model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing selected scheduling inequalities with nonnegative multipliers gives lower bounds whose supremum cannot exceed the primal optimum.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling problem is \(z^{\star}=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_k(x)\le0,\ k=1,\ldots,q\}\).
The multiplier vector satisfies \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{q}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta(\lambda)\le z^{\star}\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\), and \(d^{\star}=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\theta(\lambda)\le z^{\star}\).

children.title: Linear-Programming Scheduling Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Continuous relaxations of scheduling formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Programming Scheduling Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic LP lower-bounding relaxation of an integer minimization scheduling formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be the set of vector encodings of feasible schedules, including the required integrality and disjunctive restrictions, and let \(Q\) be a polyhedron satisfying \(P\subseteq Q\). For the minimization objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\), \[z_{\mathrm{LP}}:=\inf_{x\in Q}c^{\mathsf T}x\le \inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=:z^{\star}.\] Thus \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}\) is a lower bound on the scheduling optimum and need not be the value of a feasible schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing the feasible schedule set by a containing polyhedron yields an LP optimum no larger than the true minimization optimum.
assumptions_latex: A minimization scheduling formulation has objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) and feasible integer set \(P\).
A tractable polyhedron \(Q\) satisfies \(P\subseteq Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}:=\inf_{x\in Q}c^{\mathsf T}x\le z^{\star}:=\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\).

notation.meaning: Feasible schedules encoded as integer vectors

children.title: Surrogate Scheduling Bounds
children.top_down_role: Bounds obtained from aggregated or substituted scheduling restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate Scheduling Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative surrogate aggregation of scheduling constraints in a minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in\mathbb R_+^q\setminus\{0\}\), replace the inequalities \(g_k(x)\le0\), \(k=1,\ldots,q\), by the surrogate inequality \(\sum_{k=1}^{q}u_k g_k(x)\le0\). The surrogate value \[z(u):=\inf\left\{f(x):x\in X,\ \sum_{k=1}^{q}u_k g_k(x)\le0\right\}\] satisfies \(z(u)\le z^{\star}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative weighted aggregation of the scheduling constraints defines a relaxation whose minimization optimum is a lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The minimization problem is \(z^{\star}=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g_k(x)\le0,\ k=1,\ldots,q\}\).
The aggregation weights satisfy \(u\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{q}\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z(u):=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ \sum_k u_k g_k(x)\le0\}\le z^{\star}\).
