children.title: Schedule Verification Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Schedules, bounds, dominance records, and solver artifacts supporting solution claims.

children.title: Schedule Feasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Schedules and validation artifacts supporting constraint-satisfaction claims.

assumptions_latex: The instance data specify jobs, eligible resources, processing times, release dates, and precedence or capacity constraints.
A proposed deterministic nonpreemptive schedule specifies each job's assigned resource and start time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule is feasible exactly when all local domain, timing, precedence, and resource nonoverlap checks succeed.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit assignments and start times permit direct constraint evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct feasibility certificate for deterministic, nonpreemptive, resource-constrained schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasibility certificate is the vector \((a_j,s_j)_{j\in J}\). A verifier computes \(C_j=s_j+p_{a_jj}\) and checks: \(a_j\) is eligible; \(s_j\ge r_j\); every precedence arc \((i,j)\) satisfies \(C_i\le s_j\); and any distinct jobs \(i,j\) assigned to the same unary resource satisfy \(C_i\le s_j\) or \(C_j\le s_i\). For cumulative resources, the verifier instead checks that total demand never exceeds capacity. The certificate is accepted if and only if every specified instance constraint passes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assignments and start times certify feasibility when a verifier can directly check eligibility, releases, precedences, and resource capacities or nonoverlap.
knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Feasibility Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role and direct checks fit the leaf, but no scheduling-specific source supports the asserted complete verification conditions, especially the cumulative-resource variant.

children.title: Schedule Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Solution artifacts paired with bounds supporting optimality claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-feasibility plus matching lower-bound certificate for exact scheduling optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimality certificate for a minimization scheduling problem consists of a verifiably feasible schedule of value \(U\) and a verifiably valid global lower bound \(L\le z^{\star}\). If \(L=U\), the certificate establishes \(z^{\star}=L=U\) and global optimality of the schedule. For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the condition \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) certifies additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible schedule and a matching global lower bound certify exact optimality; a gap at most epsilon certifies additive epsilon-optimality.
assumptions_latex: The scheduling problem is a minimization problem with optimal value \(z^{\star}\).
A feasibility certificate establishes a schedule of objective value \(U\), and a valid bound certificate establishes \(L\le z^{\star}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L=U\), then \(U=z^{\star}\) and the schedule is optimal.

children.title: Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Auditable evidence supporting lower-bound or upper-bound values.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP-dual certificate for a global lower bound on a minimization scheduling problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the scheduling relaxation \[z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\},\] a vector \(y\) satisfying \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\) is a dual-feasible bound certificate. It certifies \[b^{\mathsf T}y\le z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le z^{\star}.\] Given exact \(A\), \(b\), and \(c\), verification consists of checking the two dual-feasibility inequalities and evaluating \(b^{\mathsf T}y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-feasible vector for an LP relaxation is a checkable certificate of a numerical lower bound on the original scheduling optimum.
assumptions_latex: A scheduling relaxation is \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}\) and contains every encoded feasible schedule.
A vector \(y\) satisfies \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le z^{\star}\), so \(y\) certifies the lower bound \(b^{\mathsf T}y\).

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

children.title: Dominance Records
children.top_down_role: Recorded dominance evidence supporting elimination of candidate schedules.

assumptions_latex: Two search states \(S\) and \(S'\) have the same residual scheduling state and accumulated costs \(g(S)\) and \(g(S')\).
Every feasible completion of either state has the same incremental cost when applied to the other state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(g(S)\le g(S')\), then discarding \(S'\) cannot remove a strictly better complete schedule.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: interchangeable residual states permit cost-based dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search-state dominance certificate based on identical residual possibilities and no larger accumulated cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A dominance record \((S,S')\) is valid when a verifier confirms that \(S\) and \(S'\) induce the same unscheduled jobs, resource availability, and remaining constraints, and that \(g(S)\le g(S')\). Formally, if their common completion set is \(K\) and completion \(k\in K\) adds cost \(h(k)\), then \[ g(S)+h(k)\le g(S')+h(k)\qquad\text{for every }k\in K. \] Thus every complete schedule extending \(S'\) has a no-worse counterpart extending \(S\), which certifies that pruning \(S'\) preserves at least one optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A state with the same possible completions and no smaller accumulated cost is dominated and may be pruned without losing all optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Records

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominance condition is plausible and the certificate kind fits, but no source defines the required scheduling-state equivalence. The displayed comparison and concluding pruning argument also constitute proof text.

children.title: Solver-Provenance Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Logs, statuses, and reproducibility metadata supporting scheduling claims.

assumptions_latex: A solver run acts on a fixed serialized instance and model under recorded parameters and software versions.
A collision-resistant digest function \(H\) is fixed for identifying serialized artifacts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Matching digests establish artifact identity relative to \(H\), but do not by themselves establish schedule feasibility or optimality.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reproducibility metadata and content digests identify run inputs and outputs
cryptographic validity is distinct from mathematical correctness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identity and reproducibility metadata for solver runs, distinct from mathematical certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A solver-provenance artifact is a tuple containing canonical serializations of the instance and model, their digests, solver name and version, parameter values, random seed, execution environment, termination status, timestamps, and digests of produced schedules, bounds, logs, and certificates. If \(B\) denotes any canonical serialization, its recorded identifier is \(H(B)\). Recomputing each digest and checking the tuple's internal references verifies artifact identity and linkage under the assumed digest function. These checks certify provenance consistency only; feasibility and optimality require separate mathematical certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A provenance artifact records digest-linked inputs, software, parameters, status, and outputs, enabling identity and reproducibility checks but not proving correctness.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver-Provenance Artifacts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A provenance-standard source is required. Collision resistance does not make a digest injective, so matching digests provide computational evidence of byte identity or establish equality of digest identifiers, not unconditional artifact identity.

children.title: Adaptive Scheduling Regime Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Scheduling under random processing, disruptions, partial information, rolling arrivals, and execution commitments.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Stochastic Models; Online Scheduling; Randomness, Robustness, and Reactive Scheduling

children.title: Stochastic Scheduling Decision Family
children.top_down_role: Scheduling with random processing, arrivals, failures, or other uncertain data.

children.title: Stochastic Scheduling Models
children.top_down_role: Scheduling representations with random processing, arrivals, failures, or availability.

assumptions_latex: Uncertain processing times, arrivals, capacities, or costs are random variables on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\).
Decisions at time \(t\) may depend only on the observed history represented by \(\mathcal F_t\subseteq\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stochastic scheduling model optimizes a risk functional \(\rho(C(\pi,\xi))\) over nonanticipative feasible policies \(\pi\).

notation.meaning: Risk functional applied to random cost

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stochastic control formulation uses adapted policies and a risk functional
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Policy-based stochastic scheduling model with observed-history information and general risk objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi:\Omega\to\Xi\) encode the uncertain scheduling data and let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}\) represent revealed information. A scheduling policy \(\pi=(\pi_t)_{t\ge0}\) is nonanticipative when each decision \(\pi_t\) is \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable. If \(C(\pi,\xi)\) is the resulting random cost and \(\Pi_{\mathrm{feas}}\) contains policies satisfying the scheduling constraints almost surely, the model is \[ \inf_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{feas}}}\rho\!\left(C(\pi,\xi)\right). \] Common choices include \(\rho(Y)=\mathbb E[Y]\) and tail-risk functionals; the chosen information filtration and feasibility convention are part of the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic scheduling model selects an observed-history-based policy to optimize expected or risk-adjusted random cost while satisfying constraints almost surely.
knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Scheduling Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No stochastic-scheduling source is cited. The record defines a policy-based, almost-surely feasible risk model, but its title can also encompass static decisions, chance constraints, and expectation-based feasibility; the intended subclass must be sourced and delimited.

children.title: Stochastic Scheduling Policies
children.top_down_role: Decision policies adapting scheduling choices to revealed uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Scheduling Policies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon, deterministic nonanticipative policies for stochastic scheduling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each epoch \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), let \((\mathcal H_t,\mathscr H_t)\) be the measurable space of observable histories, let \((\mathcal A_t,\mathscr A_t)\) be the measurable action space, and let \(X_t(h)\subseteq\mathcal A_t\) be the feasible actions after history \(h\in\mathcal H_t\). A stochastic scheduling policy is a sequence \(\pi=(\pi_0,\ldots,\pi_T)\) such that every rule \(\pi_t:\mathcal H_t\to\mathcal A_t\) is measurable and satisfies \(\pi_t(h)\in X_t(h)\) for every admissible history \(h\). The implemented action is \(x_t=\pi_t(H_t)\), so it depends only on the history observed through epoch \(t\) and not on subsequently revealed information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic scheduling policy assigns a feasible action to every observable history, using only information revealed by the current decision epoch.
assumptions_latex: The decision epochs are \(t=0,\ldots,T\), where \(T<\infty\).
For each \(t\), \((\mathcal H_t,\mathscr H_t)\) and \((\mathcal A_t,\mathscr A_t)\) are measurable history and action spaces.
For every admissible \(h\in\mathcal H_t\), the feasible-action set \(X_t(h)\subseteq\mathcal A_t\) is nonempty.
The random history \(H_t\) contains exactly the information observed through epoch \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t\), \(x_t=\pi_t(H_t)\in X_t(H_t)\), and histories that are identical through epoch \(t\) induce the same action.

notation.meaning: Measurable history space at epoch t
Measurable scheduling-action space at epoch t
Scheduling policy and its epoch-specific decision rules

review_flags: source_supports_stochastic-programming framework but scheduling-specific terminology remains provisional

children.title: Scenario-Based Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty representations organized around sampled or enumerated scenarios.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Based Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-scenario extensive-form scheduling with nonanticipativity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each scenario decision vector be \(x^\omega=(x_0^\omega,\ldots,x_T^\omega)\). A finite scenario-based scheduling model has the extensive form \[\min_{(x^\omega)_{\omega\in\Omega}}\ \sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega C_\omega(x^\omega)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x^\omega\in X_\omega\ \text{for every }\omega\in\Omega,\qquad x_t^\omega=x_t^{\omega'}\ \text{whenever }\omega\sim_t\omega'.\] The equality constraints impose nonanticipativity: scenario schedules may differ at epoch \(t\) only when their observed histories through that epoch differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite scenario scheduling model minimizes probability-weighted cost while requiring scenarios with identical observed histories to use identical decisions at each corresponding stage.
assumptions_latex: The common finite decision horizon is \(t=0,\ldots,T\).
The finite scenario set is \(\Omega\), with \(p_\omega>0\) and \(\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}p_\omega=1\).
For each \(\omega\in\Omega\), \(x^\omega=(x_0^\omega,\ldots,x_T^\omega)\), \(X_\omega\) is its feasible-schedule set, and \(C_\omega:X_\omega\to\mathbb R\) is its cost.
The relation \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\) means that scenarios \(\omega\) and \(\omega'\) have identical observed histories through epoch \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible solution satisfies \(x_t^\omega=x_t^{\omega'}\) for all \(t\) and all \(\omega,\omega'\in\Omega\) such that \(\omega\sim_t\omega'\).

notation.meaning: Equality of observed scenario histories through epoch t

children.title: Policy Evaluation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Performance assessment across uncertainty distributions, scenarios, or risk criteria.

assumptions_latex: Uncertain instances \(\xi^1,\ldots,\xi^N\) are sampled independently from distribution \(P\).
Policy \(\pi\) is fixed before evaluation.
The loss \(L(\pi,\xi)\) is measurable and integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat J_N(\pi)\) estimates \(J(\pi)\), while paired evaluation estimates policy differences using common instances.

notation.meaning: Scheduling loss of policy \(\pi\) on instance \(\xi\)

review_flags: available locator is indirect for out-of-sample policy evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Out-of-sample and paired evaluation of fixed scheduling policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a policy \(\pi\), its expected performance is \(J(\pi)=\mathbb E_P[L(\pi,\xi)]\). An out-of-sample evaluation on independent instances is \[\widehat J_N(\pi)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N L(\pi,\xi^n).\] When comparing \(\pi\) and \(\pi'\), paired evaluation uses the same instances and reports \(N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^N\bigl(L(\pi,\xi^n)-L(\pi',\xi^n)\bigr)\). Instances used to select or tune either policy must be separated from the evaluation sample unless selection bias is explicitly modeled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate a fixed policy on independent unseen instances; compare policies on common instances and keep tuning data separate from final evaluation data.
knowledge_statements.title: Policy Evaluation Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The evaluation formulas are mathematically standard and the principle kind fits, but the cited stochastic-programming section is indirect and does not specifically support out-of-sample testing, paired comparisons, or separation of tuning and evaluation data.

children.title: Protected Baseline Scheduling Family
children.top_down_role: Schedules designed with protection, flexibility, or uncertainty sets before execution.

children.title: Predictive Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Pre-execution scheduling driven by forecasts or nominal estimates.

assumptions_latex: All job and resource data used for planning are known estimates \(\widehat\xi\).
The deterministic feasible-schedule set is \(X(\widehat\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X(\widehat\xi)}C(x;\widehat\xi)\) is fixed before actual data are observed.
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports the predictive-scheduling definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic baseline scheduling from point forecasts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Predictive scheduling constructs a baseline schedule by solving the deterministic forecast problem \[\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X(\widehat\xi)} C(x;\widehat\xi).\] The schedule \(\bar x\) is committed before the realized data \(\xi\) are known. Forecast uncertainty affects the realized feasibility or cost of \(\bar x\), but is not represented explicitly in this optimization; any later response belongs to rescheduling or execution control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Predictive scheduling optimizes a baseline using point forecasts before actual durations, arrivals, failures, or resource availability are observed.
knowledge_statements.title: Predictive Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The point-forecast formulation is coherent, but predictive scheduling has literature-dependent meanings. A scheduling-specific source is required to establish that this exact terminal uses the stated deterministic-baseline sense.

children.title: Robust Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Pre-execution scheduling protected against specified uncertainty.

assumptions_latex: The uncertainty set \(U\) is nonempty.
For each \(\xi\in U\), \(X(\xi)\) is the feasible-schedule set.
A single baseline schedule must be selected before \(\xi\) is revealed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every optimizer \(\bar x\) is feasible for all \(\xi\in U\) and minimizes worst-case cost.
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports robust scheduling
static robust version selected; adjustable variants excluded
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static min-max robust scheduling over a prescribed uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A static robust schedule is any solution of \[\min_{x}\ \sup_{\xi\in U} C(x,\xi)\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\in\bigcap_{\xi\in U}X(\xi).\] Thus one schedule is chosen before uncertainty is revealed, remains feasible for every realization in \(U\), and minimizes its worst-case objective. This definition excludes adjustable robust schedules, whose recourse decisions may depend on subsequently observed information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A static robust schedule is feasible for every realization in a prescribed uncertainty set and minimizes the worst cost over that set.
knowledge_statements.title: Robust Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula correctly describes static min-max robust scheduling and excludes adjustable recourse, but no cited source supports selecting this particular robust-scheduling variant for the terminal.

children.title: Schedule Buffering
children.top_down_role: Temporal or capacity protection embedded in baseline schedules.

assumptions_latex: A precedence graph \(G=(V,E)\) is acyclic.
Each activity \(i\) has nominal duration \(p_i\geq0\).
Each precedence arc \((i,j)\) receives buffer \(b_{ij}\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible buffered baseline satisfies \(s_j-s_i-p_i\geq b_{ij}\) for all \((i,j)\in E\).
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports schedule buffering
resource-buffer and project-buffer variants are outside this representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-buffer representation on precedence arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A buffered baseline assigns nonnegative protection \(b_{ij}\) to precedence arcs and imposes \[s_j\geq s_i+p_i+b_{ij}\qquad((i,j)\in E).\] The realized slack protecting successor \(j\) from delay of predecessor \(i\) is \(s_j-s_i-p_i\), which is at least \(b_{ij}\). Buffers consume temporal capacity and may increase planned completion time; setting every \(b_{ij}=0\) recovers the unbuffered precedence model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schedule buffering inserts nonnegative time margins between precedence-linked activities, protecting successors from upstream delay while potentially lengthening the baseline.
knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Buffering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The precedence-arc time-buffer representation is internally coherent and representation is an appropriate kind, but schedule buffering also includes project, feeding, and resource-buffer variants. A source is needed for the chosen local sense and its claims about protection and completion time.

children.title: Flexible Baseline Schedules
children.top_down_role: Baseline schedules retaining controlled execution flexibility.

assumptions_latex: The activity set \(V\) is finite.
For every precedence arc \((i,j)\), admissible lags satisfy \(0\leq\ell_{ij}\leq u_{ij}\).
Resource constraints must hold for every schedule selected from the baseline.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any realization satisfying the lag bounds and resource constraints is an admissible schedule represented by the baseline.

notation.meaning: Set of schedules represented by the baseline

review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports flexible baseline schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flexible baseline represented by bounded temporal relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flexible baseline schedule is a nonempty set \(\mathcal B\) of executable schedules rather than one start-time vector. In a bounded-lag representation, \[\mathcal B=\left\{s\in\mathbb R^{V}:\ell_{ij}\leq s_j-s_i\leq u_{ij}\ \text{for all }(i,j)\in E,\ \text{and all resource constraints hold}\right\}.\] Execution may choose any \(s\in\mathcal B\) using observed information without revising the published temporal bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flexible baseline specifies a feasible set of schedules, often through time windows or lag bounds, from which execution may choose adaptively.
knowledge_statements.title: Flexible Baseline Schedules

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-lag interpretation is plausible, but flexible baselines admit several distinct formalisms and no source selects this one. The statement also uses the arc set E without explicitly introducing it.

children.title: Protection-Performance Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between nominal performance and uncertainty protection.

assumptions_latex: The design set of protected baselines is \(B\neq\varnothing\).
Performance loss \(P:B\to\mathbb R\) and disruption loss \(R:B\to\mathbb R\) are finite.
Both losses are minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b^*\) is Pareto efficient exactly when no \(b\in B\) weakly improves both losses and strictly improves at least one.
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports the scheduling tradeoff
generic Pareto formulation requires domain-specific sourcing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto formulation of nominal performance versus disruption protection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A protected baseline \(b^*\in B\) is efficient for the protection-performance tradeoff if there is no \(b\in B\) such that \(P(b)\leq P(b^*)\) and \(R(b)\leq R(b^*)\), with at least one strict inequality. For a budget \(\rho\), an associated constrained formulation is \[\min_{b\in B}P(b)\quad\text{subject to}\quad R(b)\leq\rho.\] Varying \(\rho\) generates supported or unsupported efficient points depending on the attainable loss set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A protected baseline is efficient when no other baseline improves nominal performance and disruption protection simultaneously, with one improvement strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Protection-Performance Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto condition is standard and property is a plausible kind, but no scheduling-specific source supports the selected performance and disruption losses or the claim about generating supported and unsupported efficient points by varying the budget.

children.title: Reactive Rescheduling
children.top_down_role: Schedule revision following failures, delays, cancellations, or resource changes.

assumptions_latex: A disruption occurs at decision epoch \(\tau\).
The observed state is \(H_\tau\), and feasible continuation schedules form \(X(H_\tau)\).
The published baseline is \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The repaired schedule is feasible for the observed state and minimizes the selected combination of operational loss and baseline deviation.
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports reactive rescheduling
objective and freezing conventions vary by application
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-triggered repair with frozen completed decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given disruption history \(H_\tau\), freeze every completed or irrevocably started decision, update durations, cancellations, and resource availability, and solve \[x^+\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X(H_\tau)}\bigl(C(x;H_\tau)+\lambda D(x,\bar x)\bigr),\qquad \lambda\geq0.\] Publish \(x^+\) as the new continuation schedule. Repeat only after the next designated trigger, or stop when all jobs are completed. The feasible set \(X(H_\tau)\) must preserve frozen decisions and enforce the updated scheduling constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a disruption, freeze irrevocable decisions, update the instance, and optimize a feasible continuation balancing operating performance against deviation from the baseline.
knowledge_statements.title: Reactive Rescheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is appropriate for the event-triggered repair procedure, but freezing rules, trigger semantics, and the scalarized repair objective vary substantially by application. No source supports this exact algorithmic variant.

children.title: Online Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Scheduling before complete job or processing information is available.

assumptions_latex: Jobs and their data are revealed sequentially.
At epoch \(t\), only history \(H_t\) is available.
Accepted decisions cannot use future arrivals or future processing information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An online algorithm produces feasible nonanticipative actions; its quality may be measured by a competitive ratio against an offline optimum.

notation.meaning: Cost incurred by algorithm \(A\) on input sequence \(\sigma\)

review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports online scheduling
competitive criterion is included as an optional evaluation convention
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential scheduling under incomplete future information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An online scheduling algorithm \(A\) selects \(x_t=A_t(H_t)\) whenever new information is revealed, with \(x_t\) feasible for the currently known instance and measurable with respect to \(H_t\). It cannot depend on unrevealed jobs or data. For a minimization problem, \(A\) is \(\alpha\)-competitive with additive constant \(\beta\geq0\) if \[C_A(\sigma)\leq\alpha C_{\mathrm{OPT}}(\sigma)+\beta\] for every admissible input sequence \(\sigma\), where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) knows the entire sequence in advance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Online scheduling makes feasible decisions as jobs or data arrive, without future information; competitive analysis compares it with a fully informed offline optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Online Scheduling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The terminal sense is broadly correct, but measurability with respect to H_t is not formally well typed without a generated sigma-field. The record also combines the definition of online scheduling with a competitive-analysis bound, and no source supports either formulation here.

children.title: Schedule Deviation-Performance Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between performance and deviation from executing or published schedules.

children.title: Schedule Stability
children.top_down_role: Preservation of timing, assignment, or sequence commitments during rescheduling.

assumptions_latex: The baseline and revised schedules assign start times \(\bar s_i\) and \(s_i\) to jobs \(i\in V\).
Weights satisfy \(w_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_{i\in V}w_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_w(s,\bar s)=0\) exactly when every positively weighted start time is unchanged.
review_flags: stability locator is indirect and not scheduling-specific
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted absolute start-time deviation as schedule instability.

source_refs.source_title: Bilevel Programming Problems: Theory, Algorithms and Applications to Energy Networks

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For baseline start times \(\bar s\) and revised start times \(s\), weighted schedule instability is \[S_w(s,\bar s)=\sum_{i\in V}w_i\lvert s_i-\bar s_i\rvert.\] It is nonnegative, equals zero precisely when \(s_i=\bar s_i\) for every job with \(w_i>0\), and satisfies the triangle inequality as a weighted seminorm of the start-time difference. Schedule stability increases as \(S_w\) decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Schedule instability can be measured by weighted absolute changes in job start times; smaller deviation means greater stability.
knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Stability

source_witnesses.source_title: Bilevel Programming Problems: Theory, Algorithms and Applications to Energy Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted absolute-deviation formula and its seminorm properties are correct, but the cited bilevel-programming stability section is not scheduling-specific and does not establish this metric as schedule stability.

children.title: Schedule Repair Cost
children.top_down_role: Operational or organizational costs induced by schedule changes.

assumptions_latex: Baseline schedule \(\bar x\) and repaired schedule \(x\) concern the same finite job set \(V\).
Start-change costs \(c_i\geq0\), reassignment costs \(d_i\geq0\), and cancellation costs \(e_i\geq0\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x,\bar x)\) is a directly computable nonnegative cost of implementing the repair.
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports schedule repair cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive implementation cost for timing, assignment, and cancellation changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An additive schedule-repair cost can be represented as \[R(x,\bar x)=\sum_{i\in V}\left(c_i\lvert s_i(x)-s_i(\bar x)\rvert+d_i\mathbf 1\{r_i(x)\neq r_i(\bar x)\}+e_i\mathbf 1\{z_i(x)>z_i(\bar x)\}\right).\] The three terms charge, respectively, start-time movement, resource reassignment, and newly introduced cancellation. With nonnegative coefficients, \(R(x,\bar x)\geq0\), and the value is computable directly from the two schedules and the declared change costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repair cost adds explicit charges for moving start times, changing assigned resources, and newly cancelling jobs relative to the baseline.
knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Repair Cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive expression is a coherent repair-cost representation, and its nonnegativity follows from the stated coefficients. A source is nevertheless required because the included timing, reassignment, and cancellation components are application-dependent rather than canonical.

children.title: Baseline Deviation Measures
children.top_down_role: Measures of difference between revised schedules and published baselines.

knowledge_statements.title: Baseline Deviation Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted deviation measures for comparing a revised schedule with a fixed baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the baseline schedule be \(B=(s^0,a^0,\prec^0)\) and a revised schedule be \(S=(s,a,\prec)\) on activities \(J\). A baseline-deviation measure is any function \(D(S,B)\geq 0\) satisfying \(D(B,B)=0\). A common additive measure is \[D(S,B)=\sum_{j\in J}w_j|s_j-s_j^0|+\sum_{j\in J}u_j\mathbf{1}[a_j\neq a_j^0]+\sum_{(i,j)\in P}v_{ij}\mathbf{1}[(i\prec j)\not\leftrightarrow(i\prec^0 j)],\] where all weights are nonnegative and \(P\subseteq J\times J\) is the set of baseline order pairs whose reversal is penalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deviation is a weighted combination of start-time changes, assignment changes, and reversals of selected baseline activity orders.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(P\) are finite.
\(w_j,u_j,v_{ij}\geq 0\).

notation.meaning: start time and assignment of activity j

review_flags: Exact scheduling-stability measure requires a scheduling-specific source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but no scheduling-stability source supports the chosen components. The order term is not well-defined: it compares propositions using an ambiguous negated biconditional and does not clearly encode reversal of a baseline pair.

children.title: Performance-Stability Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between operational performance and preservation of prior commitments.

knowledge_statements.title: Performance-Stability Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto and epsilon-constraint representations of schedule quality versus baseline stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the feasible revised schedules, let \(P:F\to\mathbb{R}\) measure performance loss, and let \(D:F\to\mathbb{R}_{+}\) measure deviation from a baseline. The performance-stability frontier is \[\mathcal{E}=\{S\in F:\nexists S'\in F\text{ with }P(S')\leq P(S),\ D(S')\leq D(S),\text{ and at least one strict inequality}\}.\] Supported frontier points minimize \(P(S)+\lambda D(S)\) for some \(\lambda\geq0\). The epsilon-constraint problem \(\min_{S\in F}P(S)\) subject to \(D(S)\leq\varepsilon\) can also recover unsupported efficient points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Efficient revised schedules admit no simultaneous improvement in performance loss and baseline deviation; weighted sums or deviation budgets expose the tradeoff.
assumptions_latex: \(F\neq\varnothing\).
\(P\) and \(D\) are real-valued on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{E}\) is the set of schedules nondominated under \((P,D)\).
review_flags: Scheduling-specific support for the bicriteria formulation is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bicriteria representation fits the leaf, but it lacks a source. The weighted-sum claim also needs the usual nonnegative two-weight formulation or a qualification excluding frontier points supported only with zero weight on performance.

children.title: Scheduling Operations Interface
children.top_down_role: Interfaces connecting scheduling models and solvers to data, users, organizational workflows, and execution control.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Design and Implementation of Scheduling Systems; Examples of Implementations

children.title: Scheduling Translation Interface
children.top_down_role: Translation between operational data, scheduling models, and specialized solvers.

children.title: Operational Data Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Exchange of jobs, resources, calendars, status, and demand data.

knowledge_statements.title: Operational Data Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed ingestion and validation contract from operational systems to scheduling instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An operational data interface is a pair \((\Phi,V)\). The ingestion map \(\Phi:\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{I}\cup\{\bot\}\) converts a raw operational record \(r\in\mathcal{R}\) into a scheduling instance \(I=(J,R,p,d,c)\), or returns \(\bot\) on rejection. The validation predicate \(V(r)\) requires identifiers to be unique, mandatory fields to be present, dimensions and units to agree, and referenced activities and resources to exist. The contract is \(V(r)\Rightarrow\Phi(r)\in\mathcal{I}\) and \(\neg V(r)\Rightarrow\Phi(r)=\bot\); accepted timestamps are converted to one declared time scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface validates operational records, normalizes their units and timestamps, and either constructs a well-typed scheduling instance or rejects them.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{R}\) has a declared schema.
\(\mathcal{I}\) is the target instance class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi\) produces a valid instance exactly for records accepted by \(V\).
review_flags: Interface contract is a formal synthesis of standard data-structuring requirements.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited data-structuring sections do not establish this exact typed validation contract. The components J, R, p, d, and c of the scheduling instance are also not introduced, so a scheduling-interface source and clarified typing are required.

children.title: Scheduling Model Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Translation between domain records and solver-ready scheduling representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Model Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contract connecting scheduling instances to mathematical model objects and decoded schedules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scheduling model interface is a pair of maps \(M:\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{M}\) and \(Q:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{S}\cup\{\bot\}\). For an instance \(I\), the model \(M(I)=(X,C,f)\) declares decision variables \(X\), constraints \(C\), and objective \(f\). If \(x\) satisfies \(C\), then \(Q(x)\) must be a feasible schedule for \(I\) with objective value \(f(x)\). Completeness requires every schedule in the intended representable class to equal \(Q(x)\) for some feasible \(x\); otherwise the interface must explicitly declare the restricted class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model interface builds variables, constraints, and an objective, then decodes feasible assignments into schedules while declaring soundness and representational completeness.
assumptions_latex: \(I\in\mathcal{I}\) has passed data validation.
\(\mathcal{M}\) has defined feasibility and objective semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible model assignments decode soundly, with completeness relative to the declared schedule class.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 The concept of a model p. 3
3.4 How to build a good model p. 36

review_flags: Formal soundness and completeness clauses require source confirmation.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 The concept of a model p. 3
3.4 How to build a good model p. 36

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the interface leaf, but the cited general model-building sections do not support the stated soundness and completeness contract. The decoder must be indexed by the instance or model, and the schedule-side objective corresponding to f(x) must be defined.

children.title: Scheduling Solver Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Invocation, configuration, result retrieval, and status exchange for scheduling solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling Solver Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed request-response contract between scheduling models and optimization solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scheduling solver interface accepts a request \(q=(m,\theta,\tau)\), where \(m\) is an encoded model, \(\theta\) contains solver parameters, and \(\tau\) is a resource limit. It returns \((\sigma,x,z,b)\), where \(\sigma\in\{\mathrm{optimal},\mathrm{feasible},\mathrm{infeasible},\mathrm{unknown}\}\). If \(\sigma\) is optimal or feasible, \(x\) must satisfy the encoded constraints and \(z\) must equal its reported objective. An optimal response additionally requires a valid bound \(b=z\); an infeasible response requires a solver-supported infeasibility certificate when the backend exposes one. Unknown makes no feasibility claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solver interface defines requests, statuses, solutions, objective values, bounds, and the validity claims attached to each returned status.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) has solver-defined feasibility and objective semantics.
\(\tau\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each response status has an explicit, checkable semantic contract.
review_flags: Detailed solver-status semantics need a solver-interface source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A general constraint-programming section is insufficient for these detailed response-status and certificate semantics. In particular, b=z at optimality depends on the solver's bound convention and exact certification assumptions.

children.title: Model-Solver Translation
children.top_down_role: Mappings between scheduling constructs and specialized solver capabilities.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Solver Translation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantics-preserving encoding and decoding between an abstract scheduling model and solver format.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m=(X,C,f)\) be an abstract scheduling model. An exact model-solver translation consists of an encoder \(T:m\mapsto\widehat m\), an injection \(E\) from assignments of \(X\) to assignments of \(\widehat m\), and a decoder \(D\). Exactness requires \[x\models C\iff E(x)\models\widehat C,\qquad \widehat f(E(x))=f(x),\qquad D(E(x))=x.\] Every feasible solver assignment relevant to the declared solution class must decode to a feasible assignment of \(m\) with the same objective value. If auxiliary variables admit multiple extensions, exactness is required after projection onto \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact translation preserves and reflects feasibility, preserves objective values, and decodes solver assignments back to abstract model assignments.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) and \(\widehat m\) have defined assignment semantics.
Auxiliary variables are removed by a declared projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\), \(E\), and \(D\) preserve feasible solutions and their objective values.

source_refs.locator: 3.4.2 Ease of detecting errors in the model p. 37

review_flags: Exact encoding theorem needs a dedicated model-translation source.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4.2 Ease of detecting errors in the model p. 37

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited error-detection section does not support an exact encoding result. The solver model components hat C and hat f are not introduced explicitly, and requiring an injection E conflicts with the later allowance for multiple auxiliary-variable extensions unless a canonical extension is specified.

children.title: Human-in-the-Loop Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Interactive decision support, manual commitments, explanations, and overrides.

knowledge_statements.title: Human-in-the-Loop Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative scheduling with validated human commitments, preferences, explanations, and overrides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given instance \(I_0\), initialize the accepted commitment set \(H_0=\varnothing\). At iteration \(k\), solve the scheduling model for \(I_k\) subject to hard commitments \(H_k\), present schedule \(S_k\) and its objective and conflict explanations, and receive human input \(u_k\). Classify \(u_k\) as a hard commitment, soft preference, data correction, or override; validate it against authorization and domain rules. Update \(I_{k+1}\) and \(H_{k+1}\), recording the change. Stop when the user accepts \(S_k\), no admissible update remains, or a declared limit is reached; output the last accepted feasible schedule and audit log.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The system alternates optimization and validated human input, recording commitments, preferences, corrections, explanations, overrides, and the final accepted schedule.
assumptions_latex: Each human input has an identifiable author and authorization scope.
The scheduling model can report feasibility or conflict information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an accepted feasible schedule together with an auditable interaction history.
review_flags: A source covering interactive scheduling commitments and overrides is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is an appropriate kind for this interactive-scheduling topic, but no source supports the workflow. The stopping rules do not ensure that an accepted feasible schedule exists, so the stated output guarantee is too strong without initialization or a conditional failure outcome.

children.title: Closed-Loop Scheduling Execution Interface
children.top_down_role: Operational coordination among schedule publication, execution monitoring, and repair.

children.title: Schedule Dispatch Integration
children.top_down_role: Publication and transmission of executable scheduling decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Schedule Dispatch Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Release of eligible scheduled operations to execution systems under rolling-time control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given schedule \(S\), execution state \(e_t\), and dispatch horizon \(h\geq0\), form \(A_t\), the activities scheduled to start by \(t+h\) whose predecessors are complete, resources are available, and release conditions hold. Order \(A_t\) by the declared dispatch priority, issue at most one idempotent command for each selected activity, and record its schedule version and command identifier. A command is committed only after acknowledgement; rejection or timeout creates an execution event rather than silently changing \(S\). Repeat at each dispatch epoch until all activities finish or execution is stopped.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each dispatch epoch, eligible near-term activities are prioritized, issued once, acknowledged, and linked to their schedule version for auditability.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) assigns activities to times and required resources.
Dispatch commands have unique identifiers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only eligible activities receive traceable, idempotent execution commands.
review_flags: A scheduling-execution integration source is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dispatch algorithm fits the leaf but has no source. Issuing at most one command does not by itself establish idempotence; retry, acknowledgement, persistence, and duplicate-suppression semantics must be specified and supported.

children.title: Execution Monitoring Integration
children.top_down_role: Collection and interpretation of execution progress, delays, and disruptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Execution Monitoring Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconciliation of observed execution events with the active schedule state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the monitored state \(e_0\) from the accepted schedule version. For each timestamped event \(y_k\), validate its activity identifier, event type, timestamp, and version; discard duplicates and quarantine inconsistent events. Apply a deterministic transition \(e_{k+1}=U(e_k,y_k)\) recording starts, completions, failures, resource changes, and measured durations. Compute residuals between observed and scheduled times and evaluate declared alert predicates. Emit the updated state and any alerts atomically so that each accepted event is processed exactly once in the logical event sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validated execution events update a versioned state exactly once, producing schedule residuals and alerts for starts, completions, failures, and resource changes.
assumptions_latex: Accepted events carry unique identifiers and timestamps.
\(U\) is defined for every accepted event type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The monitored state is a deterministic reconciliation of the accepted event sequence.

notation.meaning: execution state after k accepted events

review_flags: A source for event-based schedule monitoring semantics is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the event-reconciliation contract. Unique identifiers and an atomic state/alert update alone are insufficient to guarantee exactly-once processing across failures unless durable transaction and recovery semantics are declared.

children.title: Rescheduling Integration
children.top_down_role: Transfer of execution state into schedule revision workflows.

knowledge_statements.title: Rescheduling Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-triggered construction and deployment of a revised schedule from current execution state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given baseline schedule \(S^0\), monitored state \(e_t\), and trigger predicate \(G(e_t)\), retain completed activities as fixed history and convert started activities into binding execution commitments. If \(G(e_t)\) is false, keep the active schedule. Otherwise construct a residual instance \(I_t\), optimize a revised schedule \(S^t\) over unfinished activities subject to those commitments, and compare it with continued execution of the current schedule. Deploy \(S^t\) only if it is feasible and satisfies the declared acceptance rule, including any deviation budget; assign a new version before dispatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trigger creates a residual problem, preserves executed commitments, optimizes unfinished work, and deploys a feasible revision only under an explicit acceptance rule.
assumptions_latex: \(e_t\) distinguishes completed, started, and unstarted activities.
The residual model preserves binding execution commitments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any deployed revision is feasible for the residual instance and consistent with executed history.
review_flags: A source for event-triggered rescheduling integration is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The event-triggered rescheduling algorithm fits the leaf, but it lacks a source. The comparison with continued execution and the acceptance rule are not mathematically defined, so the precise deployment semantics remain unsupported.

children.title: Execution Feedback Loops
children.top_down_role: Coordination between dispatch status, monitored events, and schedule updates.

knowledge_statements.title: Execution Feedback Loops
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-loop state estimation, trigger evaluation, rescheduling, and dispatch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scheduling execution feedback loop has state \(e_k\), observation map \(O\), estimator \(U\), scheduling policy \(\Pi\), and dispatch map \(D\). At epoch \(k\), observations satisfy \(y_k=O(e_k)\); the estimate is updated by \(\widehat e_{k+1}=U(\widehat e_k,y_k)\); the policy produces \(S_{k+1}=\Pi(\widehat e_{k+1},S_k)\); and dispatch issues \(a_{k+1}=D(S_{k+1},\widehat e_{k+1})\). Every issued action and subsequent observation is version-linked. Feasibility guards require dispatched actions to respect the current estimated commitments and resource state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monitoring updates the execution estimate, scheduling selects a revision, and dispatch applies guarded actions whose outcomes become the next observations.
assumptions_latex: Observations can be associated with schedule and command versions.
The dispatch map enforces current feasibility guards.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O\), \(U\), \(\Pi\), and \(D\) form a versioned closed scheduling-execution loop.
review_flags: A source formalizing closed-loop scheduling execution is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf but lacks a source. It does not define how dispatched action a_{k+1} changes the actual state e_k, so the displayed equations do not yet constitute a complete closed execution-feedback loop.

children.title: Temporal Constraint Network Theory
children.top_down_role: Qualitative and quantitative temporal representations, consistency principles, conditionality, uncertainty, dispatchability, explanation, and repair.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Time for Planning; Temporal Planning
Qualitative interval, qualitative point, metric point, and combined temporal CSPs

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Recent Advances in Temporal Networks for Planning and Scheduling
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: STNs; STNUs; Consistency; Controllability; Dispatchability
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Recent Advances in Temporal Networks for Planning and Scheduling

children.title: Temporal Representation Families
children.top_down_role: Canonical distinctions among point, interval, metric, qualitative, disjunctive, conditional, and uncertain temporal models.

children.title: Point-Interval Temporal Calculus
children.top_down_role: Symbolic temporal-relation calculi over points and intervals.

children.title: Qualitative Point Algebras
children.top_down_role: Symbolic temporal-relation calculi over time points.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualitative Point Algebras
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative temporal constraints over time points using order-relation atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,<)\) be a linearly ordered time domain. The qualitative point algebra has atomic relations \(\mathcal{A}=\{<,=,>\}\); an admissible binary relation is any union \(R\subseteq\mathcal{A}\). A point-algebra network consists of variables \(V\) and constraints \(x_i\,R_{ij}\,x_j\). It is satisfiable when there exists \(v:V\to T\) such that the comparison of \(v(x_i)\) and \(v(x_j)\) belongs to \(R_{ij}\) for every constraint. Converse reverses each atom, and composition contains exactly the atoms realizable by two consecutive constrained comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Point algebra constrains pairs of time points by unions of before, equal, and after; satisfiability asks for a realization in a linear order.
assumptions_latex: \((T,<)\) is a nonempty linear order.
\(V\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Network satisfiability is existence of a valuation realizing every qualitative comparison constraint.
review_flags: An authoritative temporal-reasoning source with the point-algebra definition is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind correctly match qualitative point algebra, and the mathematical statement is standard and internally coherent. An authoritative temporal-reasoning source with a specific definition or section locator is nevertheless required.

children.title: Qualitative Interval Algebras
children.top_down_role: Symbolic temporal-relation calculi over time intervals.

assumptions_latex: Intervals are nonempty ordered pairs \(I=[s_I,e_I]\) over a linearly ordered time domain, with \(s_I<e_I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every ordered pair of intervals satisfies exactly one Allen base relation, and qualitative constraints are unions of these base relations.

notation.meaning: The set of thirteen Allen base relations.
The allowed base relations between intervals I and J.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allen's finite qualitative algebra for proper intervals on a linear time axis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The qualitative interval algebra has the jointly exhaustive, pairwise disjoint base set \(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{IA}}=\{b,m,o,s,d,f,eq,bi,mi,oi,si,di,fi\}\), denoting before, meets, overlaps, starts, during, finishes, equals, and their converses. A binary qualitative constraint \(I\,R_{IJ}\,J\) uses a relation \(R_{IJ}\subseteq\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{IA}}\); it is satisfied precisely when the unique base relation holding between \(I\) and \(J\) belongs to \(R_{IJ}\). Relations are closed under union, intersection, converse, and qualitative composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allen interval algebra represents each interval pair by one of thirteen base relations; general constraints allow unions of those relations.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualitative Interval Algebras

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the interval-algebra leaf, but no source is cited for the thirteen jointly exhaustive, pairwise disjoint relations or the stated closure properties.

children.title: Point-Interval Translation
children.top_down_role: Correspondences between point-based and interval-based temporal representations.

assumptions_latex: Intervals satisfy \(s_I<e_I\) and \(s_J<e_J\) in a linearly ordered domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each Allen base relation is equivalent to the corresponding conjunction of endpoint order constraints.

notation.meaning: Start and end points of interval I.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint-order translation of the thirteen Allen base relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For intervals \(I\) and \(J\), the seven nonconverse relations translate as follows: \(I\,b\,J\iff e_I<s_J\), \(I\,m\,J\iff e_I=s_J\), \(I\,o\,J\iff s_I<s_J<e_I<e_J\), \(I\,s\,J\iff s_I=s_J<e_I<e_J\), \(I\,d\,J\iff s_J<s_I<e_I<e_J\), \(I\,f\,J\iff s_J<s_I<e_I=e_J\), and \(I\,eq\,J\iff s_I=s_J\land e_I=e_J\). For \(r\in\{b,m,o,s,d,f\}\), \(I\,r^{-1}\,J\iff J\,r\,I\). A union of interval relations translates to the disjunction of their endpoint formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allen relations translate exactly into endpoint equalities and strict inequalities; converse and disjunctive relations translate compositionally.
knowledge_statements.title: Point-Interval Translation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The endpoint translations are internally consistent and representation is the appropriate content kind, but the exact translation table requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Qualitative Expressiveness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Differences in relations expressible across qualitative temporal calculi.

assumptions_latex: Qualitative formulas use only order relations among interval endpoints and contain no distinguished metric constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pure qualitative point or interval algebra cannot define fixed metric distances or durations.

notation.meaning: A strictly increasing transformation of the time axis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between order-invariant qualitative calculi and metric temporal constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Any formula constructed solely from endpoint comparisons \(<\), \(=\), and \(>\) is invariant under every strictly increasing transformation \(\phi\): replacing each endpoint \(t\) by \(\phi(t)\) preserves its truth. Consequently, no such qualitative formula defines a fixed metric condition such as \(e_I-s_I\le 2\). For example, \(I=[0,1]\) and \(J=[2,3]\) have the same qualitative endpoint order as \(I'=[0,100]\) and \(J'=[200,300]\), while \(e_I-s_I\le2\) holds and \(e_{I'}-s_{I'}\le2\) fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Endpoint-order calculi are invariant under increasing time transformations, so they cannot express fixed durations or distance bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualitative Expressiveness Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The order-invariance boundary and counterexample are mathematically plausible and fit failure_boundary, but the expressiveness conclusion has no cited supporting source.

children.title: Metric Time-Point Networks
children.top_down_role: Quantitative temporal-difference models over event time points.

assumptions_latex: The time domain is \(\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{Q}\), and every bound is rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The network is consistent exactly when one assignment satisfies every difference bound.

notation.meaning: Finite set of temporal event variables.
Directed upper bound on a time difference.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple temporal networks represented by non-strict difference constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A metric time-point network is a pair \(N=(V,C)\), where each \(x_i\in V\) denotes an event time and every constraint in \(C\) has the form \(l_{ij}\le x_j-x_i\le u_{ij}\). Equivalently, it comprises directed difference inequalities \(x_j-x_i\le u_{ij}\) and \(x_i-x_j\le-l_{ij}\). A schedule is a map \(t:V\to\mathbb{R}\) or \(t:V\to\mathbb{Q}\); the network is consistent when some schedule satisfies all inequalities simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric time-point network constrains event-time differences by lower and upper bounds and is consistent when all bounds admit one schedule.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Time-Point Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a suitable definition of a simple metric time-point network, with the selected time domain supplied by the assumptions, but it lacks a temporal-reasoning source and inspectable locator.

children.title: Disjunctive Mixed Temporal Network Family
children.top_down_role: Temporal models admitting alternative bounds or combining metric and qualitative relations.

children.title: Disjunctive Temporal Networks
children.top_down_role: Temporal networks admitting alternatives among metric bounds or constraints.

assumptions_latex: Variables range over \(\mathbb{Q}\) or \(\mathbb{R}\), and all constants are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires satisfying at least one difference inequality from every disjunctive constraint.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjunctive temporal problems over finite unions of difference constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A disjunctive temporal network is \(N=(V,\{D_k\}_{k=1}^m)\), where each constraint is a finite disjunction \(D_k=\bigvee_{r=1}^{q_k}(x_{j_{kr}}-x_{i_{kr}}\le b_{kr})\). A schedule \(t:V\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \(D_k\) when at least one indexed inequality is true under \(t\), and it satisfies \(N\) when this holds for every \(k\). Ordinary metric time-point networks are the special case \(q_k=1\) for all \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disjunctive temporal network requires each clause to satisfy at least one of several alternative difference bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Temporal Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent for clauses of atomic difference inequalities and fits the leaf, but the precise scope of “disjunctive temporal network” varies in the literature and must be tied to a cited definition.

children.title: Mixed Temporal Networks
children.top_down_role: Temporal networks combining metric constraints with qualitative relations.

assumptions_latex: Every interval has endpoints \(s_I<e_I\), and point and endpoint variables share one linearly ordered metric domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistency means that one assignment satisfies both the metric and qualitative components.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally scoped hybrid network combining metric bounds and qualitative temporal relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed temporal network is a tuple \(N=(P,\mathcal{I},C_M,C_Q)\), where \(P\) is a finite set of time points, \(\mathcal{I}\) is a finite set of intervals represented by endpoints, \(C_M\) contains metric difference constraints over points and endpoints, and \(C_Q\) contains qualitative point or interval relations. An interpretation assigns every point a time and every interval two ordered endpoints. It is a model of \(N\) exactly when it satisfies every constraint in \(C_M\cup C_Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed temporal network uses one time assignment to satisfy metric difference bounds and qualitative point or interval relations together.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Temporal Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed hybrid semantics fits the local leaf and definition role, but “mixed temporal network” is not standardized enough to accept this exact tuple and constraint language without a selected authoritative source.

children.title: Metric-Qualitative Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interactions between numerical bounds and symbolic temporal relations.

assumptions_latex: Intervals are proper and interpreted over a linearly ordered metric domain.
Strict difference constraints are available, or a positive separation parameter \(\varepsilon\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Endpoint translation couples qualitative relations to metric constraints without introducing separate interval semantics.

notation.meaning: Positive minimum separation used to encode strict order.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling through shared interval endpoints and translated order constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every Allen base relation \(r\), impose \(I\,r\,J\) by adding its endpoint formula \(T_r(I,J)\) to the shared metric network. Equality \(x=y\) becomes \(x-y\le0\land y-x\le0\). Under an \(\varepsilon\)-separated convention, strict order \(x<y\) becomes \(x-y\le-\varepsilon\); without known positive separation over dense time, it must remain an open constraint and cannot be represented exactly by a single non-strict bound. Thus \(I\,r\,J\iff T_r(I,J)\) under the selected strictness convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualitative interval relations couple to metric networks through shared endpoints, with strict order requiring open bounds or a justified positive separation.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Qualitative Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly distinguishes dense-time strict inequalities from epsilon-separated encodings, but the claimed coupling equivalence depends on the selected strictness convention and needs a supporting source.

children.title: Disjunction Complexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes governing the difficulty introduced by temporal alternatives.

assumptions_latex: Input constants are rational and encoded in binary.
Each disjunctive clause contains finitely many difference inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Disjunctive temporal consistency is NP-complete, whereas the singleton-disjunction case is decidable in polynomial time.

notation.meaning: Total number of listed difference inequalities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision complexity for finite disjunctions of rational difference constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The consistency problem for disjunctive temporal networks is NP-complete in the binary encoding model. An NP certificate selects one inequality from each disjunction; the resulting ordinary difference-constraint system is checked in time polynomial in \(n\), \(M\), and the bound bit lengths by detecting a negative directed cycle. NP-hardness arises when unrestricted finite disjunctions are admitted. If every disjunction has one member, consistency reduces to an ordinary metric time-point network and is decidable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing disjunctions makes temporal consistency NP-complete; selecting one branch yields a polynomially checkable ordinary difference network.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunction Complexity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits the leaf, and the certificate argument is consistent with the stated clause model, but NP-completeness is a nontrivial theorem requiring an exact authoritative theorem or section locator.

children.title: Conditional Temporal Networks
children.top_down_role: Temporal networks whose relevant events and constraints depend on observations or conditions.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Dynamic Controllability of Conditional Simple Temporal Networks

assumptions_latex: The proposition set and event set are finite.
Each proposition has a designated observation event.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each complete observation scenario induces an ordinary temporal network by retaining exactly its active events and constraints.

notation.meaning: Finite set of Boolean observation propositions.
Conjunction of literals labeling an event or constraint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario semantics for conditionally present events and temporal constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conditional temporal network consists of events \(V\), propositions \(P\), observation events \(O(p)\in V\), labels \(L(v)\) on events, and labeled temporal constraints \((x_j-x_i\le b,L(c))\). A scenario \(\sigma:P\to\{\mathsf{true},\mathsf{false}\}\) activates an event or constraint exactly when \(\sigma\models L(\cdot)\). Its projection contains the active events and active constraints whose endpoints are active. A scenario schedule assigns times to all events in that projection and satisfies its active difference constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditional temporal network projects to a temporal network after observations determine which labeled events and constraints are active.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Temporal Networks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scenario-projection semantics matches the local topic broadly, but conditional temporal-network variants impose different labeling and well-definedness conditions. A specific variant and authoritative definition must be cited before the hypotheses can be judged sufficient.

children.title: Time-Domain Regime Pair
children.top_down_role: Temporal reasoning regimes distinguished by the underlying time domain.

children.title: Discrete Time Domains
children.top_down_role: Temporal reasoning over integer-valued or otherwise discretized time.

assumptions_latex: A positive time quantum \(h>0\) and origin \(t_0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All admissible event times belong to the lattice \(t_0+h\mathbb{Z}\), possibly intersected with a finite horizon.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform discrete temporal domains for event-time assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A uniform discrete time domain is \(T_h=\{t_0+kh:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}\), or \(T_h\cap[a,b]\) when a finite horizon is imposed. A temporal assignment is a map \(t:V\to T_h\). After the normalization \(z_v=(t(v)-t_0)/h\), every temporal variable is integer-valued. Difference constraints are interpreted only on these lattice assignments, so an interval containing real times but no lattice point is infeasible in the discrete model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete time model restricts every event to a fixed temporal lattice, optionally within a finite planning horizon.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Time Domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform-lattice definition is precise and fits the discrete-time leaf, but no cited source or explicit standard-field rationale supports the selected model and normalization claim.

children.title: Continuous Time Domains
children.top_down_role: Temporal reasoning over dense or real-valued time.

assumptions_latex: Time is linearly ordered and modeled by \(\mathbb{R}\), or by a specified real interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Temporal variables may take arbitrary real values, including values between any two distinct admissible times.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense real-valued temporal domains for event-time assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous time domain is \(T=\mathbb{R}\), or a real interval such as \([a,b]\subseteq\mathbb{R}\), equipped with its usual order and metric. A temporal assignment is a map \(t:V\to T\). Unlike a fixed discrete lattice, \(T\) is dense: whenever \(u,v\in T\) and \(u<v\), some \(w\in T\) satisfies \(u<w<v\). Metric difference constraints are evaluated using ordinary real subtraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous time assigns events arbitrary real values in a dense ordered domain and evaluates bounds using real differences.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Time Domains

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The real-valued dense-time definition is internally consistent and fits the leaf, but the record supplies neither a source nor explicit standard-field rationale.

children.title: Time Discretization Effects
children.top_down_role: Changes in fidelity, feasibility, or complexity caused by temporal discretization.

assumptions_latex: Discretization uses the lattice \(h\mathbb{Z}\) with \(h>0\).
The temporal model contains non-strict difference constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Grid alignment can preserve feasibility, but unaligned bounds can make discretization remove feasible continuous schedules.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility changes caused by restricting continuous schedules to a uniform grid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every bound in a feasible system \(x_j-x_i\le b_{ij}\) belongs to \(h\mathbb{Z}\), then feasibility over \(\mathbb{R}\) implies feasibility with all variables in \(h\mathbb{Z}\); scaling by \(h\) yields an integer-bound difference system. Without grid alignment, this equivalence fails. For example, \(0.4\le x-y\le0.6\) has real solutions, but no solution with \(x,y\in\mathbb{Z}\). Thus discretization may destroy feasibility unless bounds, strictness, and grid resolution satisfy an exact preservation condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Aligned difference bounds preserve feasibility on a uniform grid, while unaligned bounds can eliminate valid continuous schedules.
knowledge_statements.title: Time Discretization Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The aligned-bound preservation claim and unaligned counterexample fit failure_boundary, but real feasibility implying lattice feasibility for integral difference bounds is a substantive integrality result requiring a specific source locator.

children.title: Domain-Sensitive Temporal Reasoning
children.top_down_role: Reasoning behavior that depends on the selected underlying time domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Sensitive Temporal Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of temporal feasibility on discrete versus continuous time domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq E\) be ordered additive time domains and let \(N=(V,(S_{ij}))\) impose constraints \(t_j-t_i\in S_{ij}\). Define \(\operatorname{Sol}_D(N)=\{t\in D^V:t_j-t_i\in S_{ij}\text{ for every constrained pair }(i,j)\}\). Then \(\operatorname{Sol}_D(N)\subseteq\operatorname{Sol}_E(N)\), so continuous feasibility need not imply discrete feasibility. For a simple temporal network consisting only of inequalities \(t_j-t_i\le c_{ij}\) with integral finite bounds, however, feasibility over \(\mathbb R\) is equivalent to feasibility over \(\mathbb Z\): absence of a negative directed cycle yields an integral shortest-path potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting the time domain can destroy feasibility, although integral simple difference constraints are feasible over the reals exactly when feasible over the integers.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq E\) are ordered additive time domains.
All finite bounds \(c_{ij}\) in the stated equivalence are integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Sol}_D(N)\subseteq\operatorname{Sol}_E(N)\), and for integral simple difference constraints, \(\operatorname{Sol}_{\mathbb R}(N)\ne\varnothing\iff\operatorname{Sol}_{\mathbb Z}(N)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: solutions of network N whose time values lie in D
allowed temporal differences from variable i to variable j

review_flags: Exact source for the mixed discrete-continuous formulation and integral-potential equivalence is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The domain inclusion and integral difference-constraint claim are mathematically plausible and fit the principle container, but the mixed discrete/continuous equivalence has no cited support.
