Without finite lower-level bounds, no finite weight universally prevents such an override.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite weights reproduce lexicographic priority only when each level outweighs every possible aggregate improvement below it; unbounded lower losses defeat any finite weight.
assumptions_latex: \(G_k(r)\) is integer-valued with \(0\le G_k(r)\le B_k\).
\(W_k>0\) for every priority level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(W_k>\sum_{j>k}W_jB_j\) prevent lower-priority override; their failure permits override instances.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the exact dominance-weight boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits Priority Override Boundaries, and the displayed dominance inequalities are a plausible universal sufficient condition under bounded integer losses. Because no source is supplied, the exact sufficiency, the existential override claim when an inequality fails, and the unbounded-loss boundary remain unsupported.

children.title: Minimal-Change Reconfiguration
children.top_down_role: Repair centered on preserving prior choices, installed components, or operational continuity.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Change Reconfiguration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repair minimizing deviation from a fixed incumbent configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a configuration space, let \(F\subseteq X\) be the nonempty set satisfying all hard post-change constraints, and let \(x^0\in X\) be the incumbent configuration. Given a deviation measure \(d:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}_+\), a minimal-change reconfiguration is any \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}d(x,x^0).\] For componentwise configurations, a standard choice is weighted Hamming deviation \(d(x,x^0)=\sum_jw_j\mathbf{1}[x_j\ne x_j^0]\), which counts changed components while allowing different preservation costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among configurations satisfying the new hard constraints, choose one with minimum measured deviation from the incumbent configuration.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty.
The minimum of \(d(x,x^0)\) over \(F\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) is feasible and no \(x\in F\) is closer to \(x^0\) under \(d\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports minimal-change reconfiguration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the topic role of preserving an incumbent configuration and explicitly assumes feasibility and attainment. No source with a specific locator supports either the minimal-deviation formulation or weighted Hamming deviation as the stated standard choice.

children.title: Stakeholder Preference Reconfiguration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Repairs tailored to individual or multiple stakeholder preferences.

children.title: Personalized Reconfiguration
children.top_down_role: Repairs tailored to the preferences of an individual user.

knowledge_statements.title: Personalized Reconfiguration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible repair optimized for one stakeholder’s elicited preferences and change costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the nonempty set of feasible reconfigurations for an incumbent \(x^0\), and let stakeholder \(u\) have preference loss \(L_u:F\to\mathbb{R}\) and change-cost function \(d_u:F\times X\to\mathbb{R}_+\). For a fixed tradeoff parameter \(\lambda_u\ge0\), a personalized reconfiguration for \(u\) is any \[x_u^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}\bigl(L_u(x)+\lambda_ud_u(x,x^0)\bigr).\] Personalization is stakeholder-specific because either the loss, change cost, or tradeoff parameter may differ between stakeholders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A personalized repair minimizes one stakeholder’s preference loss together with that stakeholder’s cost of changing the incumbent configuration.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty.
The personalized objective attains its minimum on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_u^*\) minimizes \(L_u(x)+\lambda_ud_u(x,x^0)\) over all \(x\in F\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports personalized reconfiguration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is locally relevant, but no source supports the additive scalarization chosen as the meaning of personalized reconfiguration. The statement also does not explicitly declare the stakeholder domain containing u or state x^0 in X, even though d_u has domain F times X.

children.title: Group Reconfiguration
children.top_down_role: Repairs produced for multiple affected stakeholders.

knowledge_statements.title: Group Reconfiguration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint feasible repair selected from losses reported by a finite stakeholder group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a finite nonempty stakeholder set, \(F\) a nonempty set of feasible reconfigurations, and \(L_u:F\to\mathbb{R}\) the loss of stakeholder \(u\). Given a nondecreasing aggregation function \(A:\mathbb{R}^{|U|}\to\mathbb{R}\), a group reconfiguration is any \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}A\bigl((L_u(x))_{u\in U}\bigr).\] The chosen aggregator is part of the regime and determines how improvements and losses across different stakeholders may compensate one another.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A group repair minimizes an explicitly chosen aggregation of all stakeholders’ losses over the common feasible configuration set.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and nonempty, and \(F\) is nonempty.
The aggregate objective attains its minimum on \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) is feasible and aggregate-loss minimal for the specified group rule \(A\).

notation.meaning: stakeholder u's loss at configuration x

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports group reconfiguration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Group Reconfiguration and identifies aggregation as regime-dependent. It has no supporting citation, and 'nondecreasing' should be tied explicitly to the coordinatewise order on stakeholder-loss vectors.

children.title: Stakeholder Preference Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Combination of differing stakeholder preferences for repair selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Stakeholder Preference Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar representations of stakeholder loss profiles for group repair selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite stakeholder set \(U\), let \(L(x)=(L_u(x))_{u\in U}\) be the loss profile of feasible reconfiguration \(x\in F\). Three standard scalar aggregations are \[A_{\mathrm{sum}}(L)=\sum_{u\in U}\alpha_uL_u,\qquad A_{\max}(L)=\max_{u\in U}\alpha_uL_u,\qquad A_{\mathrm{nash}}(L)=-\sum_{u\in U}\alpha_u\log(b_u-L_u),\] where \(\alpha_u>0\), and the Nash form requires \(L_u<b_u\). Each group rule selects an element of \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}A(L(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stakeholder loss profiles may be aggregated by weighted total loss, worst weighted loss, or a Nash-style logarithmic objective.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and \(\alpha_u>0\).
For the Nash form, \(L_u(x)<b_u\) on its admissible domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}A(L(x))\) is the repair induced by the chosen aggregation rule.

notation.meaning: stakeholder-specific reference loss for Nash aggregation

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the stakeholder aggregation formulas.
The Nash-style loss convention requires source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits Stakeholder Preference Aggregation, but no source supports the three selected formulas. In particular, the logarithmic expression is a Nash-style product of positive slacks b_u-L_u under a loss convention, so its interpretation and the role of b_u require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Stakeholder Fairness Criteria
children.top_down_role: Distribution of repair benefits and burdens across participants.

knowledge_statements.title: Stakeholder Fairness Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Checkable Pareto, anonymity, and max-loss fairness predicates for group repairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(x)=(L_u(x))_{u\in U}\) be stakeholder losses on a feasible set \(F\). A repair \(x^*\in F\) is Pareto fair if no \(y\in F\) satisfies \(L_u(y)\le L_u(x^*)\) for all \(u\) with one strict inequality. An aggregation rule is anonymous if permuting stakeholder labels leaves its value unchanged. A repair is minimax fair if \[x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}\max_{u\in U}L_u(x).\] These criteria are distinct and must be declared separately when evaluating a group regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group repairs can be tested for Pareto efficiency, invariance to stakeholder labels, and minimization of the worst individual loss.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite and nonempty.
All stakeholder losses are evaluated on the same feasible set \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed predicates respectively characterize Pareto fairness, anonymity, and minimax fairness.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the selected fairness predicates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is appropriate for a criteria leaf, and the three predicates are kept distinct. No source supports the selected fairness notions or the terminology 'Pareto fair'; a cited treatment should also establish the intended meaning of anonymity and minimax fairness.

children.title: Multiobjective Repair Portfolio Regimes
children.top_down_role: Presentation of nondominated or deliberately diverse repair alternatives.

children.title: Pareto-Optimal Reconfiguration
children.top_down_role: Repair alternatives retained because no competing repair improves every objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Pareto-Optimal Reconfiguration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong Pareto efficiency for finite-dimensional repair-objective vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a nonempty feasible reconfiguration set and let \(f:F\to\mathbb{R}^m\) collect objectives to be minimized. A repair \(x^*\in F\) is Pareto-optimal if there is no \(x\in F\) such that \(f_i(x)\le f_i(x^*)\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(f_j(x)<f_j(x^*)\) for at least one index \(j\). The Pareto repair set consists of all such nondominated feasible configurations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reconfiguration is Pareto-optimal when no feasible alternative improves at least one objective without worsening another.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty.
Every component of \(f\) is interpreted as a minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\) belongs to the Pareto set exactly when no feasible objective vector strongly dominates \(f(x^*)\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports multiobjective Pareto reconfiguration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed nondominance definition fits Pareto-Optimal Reconfiguration and agrees with the plain statement. No source is supplied, and the conclusion calls componentwise weak improvement with at least one strict improvement 'strong domination,' terminology that is not uniform and can instead mean strict improvement in every component. A source is needed to fix the convention reliably.

children.title: Diverse Repair Portfolios
children.top_down_role: Collections of deliberately varied repair alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Diverse Repair Portfolios
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a finite portfolio satisfying quality and pairwise repair-separation requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be a finite set of feasible repairs, let \(Q\subseteq R\) contain the repairs meeting prescribed quality bounds, and let \(d:R\times R\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) be a symmetric dissimilarity with \(d(r,r)=0\). For a portfolio-size limit \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and separation threshold \(\delta\ge 0\), a diverse repair portfolio is a set \(P\subseteq Q\) such that \(1\le |P|\le k\) and
\[\min_{\substack{r,s\in P\\r\ne s}}d(r,s)\ge\delta,\]
where the minimum condition is vacuous when \(|P|=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diverse portfolio contains quality-admissible repairs whose pairwise dissimilarities meet a prescribed threshold and whose cardinality respects a portfolio limit.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) and \(Q\) are finite.
\(d\) is a nonnegative symmetric dissimilarity with zero diagonal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subseteq Q\), \(1\le |P|\le k\), and \(d(r,s)\ge\delta\) for all distinct \(r,s\in P\).

notation.meaning: Portfolio, size limit, and separation threshold.

review_flags: Multiple portfolio-diversity conventions exist; a direct source for this threshold-separated formulation is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but the threshold-separated portfolio convention is not uniquely standard and no source is cited.

children.title: Objective Tradeoff Coverage
children.top_down_role: Coverage of materially different compromises among repair objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Tradeoff Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses additive componentwise coverage of the attainable Pareto objective image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be a finite feasible repair set and let \(f:R\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be minimized componentwise. Write \(R^{\mathrm{ND}}\) for the nondominated repairs. Given a tolerance vector \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^m\), a portfolio \(P\subseteq R\) provides additive \(\varepsilon\)-tradeoff coverage when
\[\forall r\in R^{\mathrm{ND}}\;\exists p\in P\;\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\quad f_i(p)\le f_i(r)+\varepsilon_i.\]
Thus every nondominated objective vector is componentwise approximated by at least one represented repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A portfolio covers objective tradeoffs when every nondominated repair is componentwise approximated, within specified additive tolerances, by a portfolio member.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is finite and nonempty.
Every component of \(f\) is interpreted as a minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) additively \(\varepsilon\)-covers the nondominated objective image \(f(R^{\mathrm{ND}})\).

notation.meaning: Vector of repair objectives to minimize.

review_flags: A direct multiobjective approximation source is needed for the selected additive coverage convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive componentwise coverage formula is precise and matches the title, but alternative tradeoff-coverage conventions exist and no source supports this selected definition.

children.title: Repair Diversity Criteria
children.top_down_role: Criteria for distinguishing alternatives by decisions, outcomes, or stakeholder impact.

knowledge_statements.title: Repair Diversity Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies a weighted change-set distance and its portfolio-level separation predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be the finite set of configurable decisions, let \(\Delta(r)\subseteq U\) be the decisions changed by repair \(r\), and assign weights \(w_u>0\). Define
\[d_w(r,s)=\sum_{u\in\Delta(r)\mathbin{\triangle}\Delta(s)}w_u.\]
For a portfolio \(P\) and threshold \(\delta\ge0\), the weighted change-set diversity criterion is
\[\operatorname{Div}_{\delta}(P)\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\forall r,s\in P,\ r\ne s:\ d_w(r,s)\ge\delta.\]
The criterion compares repair interventions rather than merely their objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repairs are diverse when every pair differs on changed configuration decisions by at least a prescribed total weight.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is finite.
\(w_u>0\) for every \(u\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Div}_{\delta}(P)\) holds exactly when every distinct repair pair has weighted symmetric-difference distance at least \(\delta\).

notation.meaning: Configuration decisions changed by repair r.

review_flags: Repair diversity admits several inequivalent metrics; this change-set criterion needs direct sourcing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted symmetric-difference condition is internally consistent and appropriately classified as a condition, but its use as the repair-diversity criterion requires direct evidence.

children.title: Planning-Scheduling-Configuration Coupling
children.top_down_role: Joint models and coordination architectures in which plan structure, temporal-resource feasibility, and configuration decisions are mutually dependent.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Integrating Planning and Scheduling
Constraint-Based Scheduling and Planning; Integration of CP and OR

children.title: Coupled Problem Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem families distinguished by which planning, scheduling, resource, and configuration decisions are jointly endogenous.

children.title: Plan-Schedule Coupling
children.top_down_role: Joint action selection, ordering, timing, and resource allocation.

children.title: Joint Action Selection
children.top_down_role: Action choices evaluated together with downstream schedulability.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Action Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary action selection is shared by planning, temporal, and resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For candidate actions \(A\), introduce \(x_a\in\{0,1\}\), with \(x_a=1\) exactly when action \(a\) belongs to the plan. A joint action-selection formulation has feasible set
\[X=\{x\in\{0,1\}^{A}:x\in X_{\mathrm{logic}},\ \exists(s,z)\text{ such that }(x,s,z)\in X_{\mathrm{time}}\cap X_{\mathrm{resource}}\}.\]
Here \(X_{\mathrm{logic}}\) enforces planning support, transition, and goal requirements; \(s\) gives temporal placements; and \(z\) gives resource assignments. An action vector is jointly admissible precisely when its selected actions admit both a valid plan interpretation and a feasible schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Actions are selected once, and selection is feasible only when it satisfies planning logic and admits compatible temporal and resource assignments.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite candidate-action set.
The planning, temporal, and resource constraint sets use the same selection variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X\) if and only if \(x\) is planning-feasible and extends to a feasible schedule and resource allocation.

notation.meaning: Binary selection variable for action a.

review_flags: The locator supports constraint-model composition provisionally; direct integrated planning-scheduling support should be checked.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is coherent and fits joint action selection, but a generic constraint-programming section does not specifically support the asserted integrated planning, temporal, and resource feasible-set representation.

children.title: Temporal Placement of Planned Actions
children.top_down_role: Mapping planned actions into temporally feasible placements.

knowledge_statements.title: Temporal Placement of Planned Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optional planned actions receive starts, ends, and precedence-consistent temporal placements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each action \(a\) with duration \(p_a>0\), let \(x_a\in\{0,1\}\) indicate selection and let \(s_a,e_a\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) be its start and end. Temporal placement requires \(e_a=s_a+p_a\) whenever \(x_a=1\). For every required precedence \((a,b)\), impose
\[x_a=x_b=1\;\Longrightarrow\;e_a\le s_b.\]
If actions \(a\) and \(b\) cannot overlap, impose
\[x_a=x_b=1\;\Longrightarrow\;(e_a\le s_b)\lor(e_b\le s_a).\]
A placement is feasible when all selected actions satisfy these relations and any stated release dates or deadlines.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each selected action receives a duration-consistent interval satisfying required precedences, nonoverlap restrictions, and applicable time windows.
assumptions_latex: Action durations \(p_a\) are positive and fixed.
Precedence and incompatibility relations are specified over candidate actions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected actions form a temporally feasible schedule exactly when suitable \((s,e)\) satisfy all displayed implications and time windows.

notation.meaning: Start and end times of action a.

review_flags: The exact optional-interval formulation should be confirmed against a scheduling source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The temporal constraints are standard and precise, but the cited generic constraint-programming locator does not establish the optional-action interval and nonoverlap formulation used here.

children.title: Resource Allocation Across Planned Activities
children.top_down_role: Allocation of shared resources to activities induced by a plan.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Allocation Across Planned Activities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a cumulative renewable-capacity condition for selected, temporally placed activities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be a finite set of renewable resources. Selected activity \(a\) occupies the half-open interval \([s_a,e_a)\) and consumes \(q_{ar}\ge0\) units of resource \(r\). With capacity \(C_r\ge0\), an allocation is resource-feasible exactly when
\[\forall r\in R\;\forall t\ge0:\quad \sum_{a:x_a=1,\ s_a\le t<e_a}q_{ar}\le C_r.\]
If activity modes are selectable, \(q_{ar}\) and the duration are those of the chosen mode. The condition couples action selection and temporal overlap through simultaneous resource demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every time, the total demand of selected activities executing then cannot exceed the capacity of any renewable resource.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) and the candidate-activity set are finite.
Resource capacities and activity demands are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule is renewable-resource feasible if and only if every resource-time capacity inequality holds.

notation.meaning: Demand of activity a for resource r.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

review_flags: The locator is provisionally relevant to resource allocation; the cumulative-time formulation requires confirmation.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.1 Resource allocation in production planning p. 4

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The renewable-capacity condition is mathematically sound and fits the leaf, but the cited production-planning resource-allocation locator is insufficiently specific to support the continuous-time cumulative formulation.

children.title: Plan–Schedule Feasibility Feedback
children.top_down_role: Feedback from scheduling feasibility into planning decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Plan–Schedule Feasibility Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scheduling conflict becomes a verifiable nogood over planning selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_a\in\{0,1\}\) denote planned-action selection. Suppose a scheduling solver returns a conflict set \(C\) such that no temporal and resource assignment is feasible whenever every action in \(C\) is selected. Then
\[\sum_{a\in C}x_a\le |C|-1\]
is a valid plan-level nogood. The pair consisting of \(C\) and a scheduling infeasibility certificate for the restrictions induced by \(C\) certifies the feedback cut. Adding the nogood excludes the conflicting joint selection and every plan containing it, while retaining selections that omit at least one member of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified unschedulable action subset yields a nogood preventing the planner from selecting all actions in that subset again.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is scheduling-infeasible independently of actions outside \(C\).
The scheduling solver supplies a checkable infeasibility certificate for \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{a\in C}x_a\le |C|-1\) is valid for every jointly plan-schedule-feasible solution.
review_flags: A direct source is needed for conflict extraction and the claimed plan-level feedback certificate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the stated independence assumption, the nogood is valid and the certificate content kind fits the leaf. A direct source is nevertheless required for the conflict-certificate feedback construction.

children.title: Configuration-Dependent Planning
children.top_down_role: Planning in which available actions and capabilities depend on selected components.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration-Dependent Planning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines planning whose action availability is controlled by selected configuration components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\) be configurable components, \(A\) candidate actions, and \(y_j,x_a\in\{0,1\}\) indicate selected components and actions. Given capability incidences \(h_{aj}\in\{0,1\}\), configuration-dependent planning imposes
\[x_a\le\sum_{j\in J}h_{aj}y_j\qquad(a\in A),\]
together with configuration feasibility \(y\in Y\) and the ordinary state-transition, support, ordering, and goal constraints on \(x\). More generally, each action may have a Boolean availability predicate \(H_a(y)\), enforced by \(x_a\le H_a(y)\). Thus the chosen configuration determines which planning operators or capabilities can participate in a valid plan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A configuration-dependent plan selects only actions enabled by chosen components while also satisfying configuration, transition, support, ordering, and goal constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and \(A\) are finite.
\(Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\) describes feasible configurations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every selected action is enabled by the selected configuration, and the selected actions constitute a valid plan.

notation.meaning: Selection indicator for configuration component j.
Whether component j supplies capability for action a.

review_flags: Network-design activation is analogous; direct configuration-dependent planning evidence remains desirable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the node role, but network-design activation is only analogous and does not directly support configuration-dependent planning or the stated action-availability formulation.

children.title: Configuration-Dependent Scheduling
children.top_down_role: Scheduling in which capacities, routes, modes, or machines are design decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Configuration-Dependent Scheduling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines scheduling with configuration-controlled capacities, machines, routes, or execution modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y\in Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{J}\) select a feasible configuration. For each activity \(a\), let \(M_a(y)\) be the modes enabled by \(y\), and for each resource \(r\), let \(C_r(y)\) be the installed capacity. A configuration-dependent schedule chooses a mode \(m_a\in M_a(y)\) and times \(s_a,e_a\) for every selected activity, satisfies its mode-dependent duration and precedence constraints, and obeys
\[\forall r\;\forall t:\quad \sum_{a:s_a\le t<e_a}q_{ar}(m_a)\le C_r(y).\]
Consequently, changing \(y\) can alter scheduling feasibility through available machines, routes, modes, durations, or capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The selected configuration determines available execution modes and capacities, so schedule feasibility depends directly on design choices.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a finite configuration set.
Enabled modes, demands, durations, and installed capacities are defined for each feasible configuration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A schedule is feasible under \(y\) exactly when all activities use enabled modes and satisfy temporal and configuration-dependent capacity constraints.

notation.meaning: Modes enabled for activity a by configuration y.
Installed capacity of resource r under configuration y.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.5 Set Covering with Many Variables: Crew Scheduling p. 57

review_flags: The two locators provisionally support scheduling and design activation; their integrated formulation requires checking.

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4.5 Set Covering with Many Variables: Crew Scheduling p. 57

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition coherently captures configuration-controlled modes and capacities, but separate crew-scheduling and network-design locators do not establish the integrated configuration-dependent scheduling formulation.

children.title: Planning–Scheduling–Configuration Co-Design
children.top_down_role: Simultaneous system design and operational decision making.

knowledge_statements.title: Planning–Scheduling–Configuration Co-Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines simultaneous design, plan, and schedule optimization in one coupled feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y\) denote configuration decisions, \(x\) planning decisions, and \(z\) scheduling decisions. Planning–scheduling–configuration co-design is the optimization problem
\[\min_{(y,x,z)}\;F(y,x,z)\quad\text{subject to}\quad y\in Y,\quad (x,y)\in P,\quad (z,x,y)\in S.\]
Here \(Y\) enforces configuration feasibility, \(P\) enforces plan validity and configuration-dependent action availability, and \(S\) enforces temporal, mode, and resource feasibility for the planned actions under the chosen configuration. The formulation is simultaneous: no block is fixed before optimizing the others, and the objective may combine design cost with operational plan and schedule performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Co-design jointly chooses system components, planned actions, and their schedule while enforcing all cross-domain feasibility constraints and optimizing combined performance.
assumptions_latex: The feasible sets \(Y\), \(P\), and \(S\) are explicitly specified.
\(F\) is defined on every jointly feasible triple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any feasible solution \((y,x,z)\) is simultaneously configuration-feasible, plan-valid, and schedulable under the selected configuration.

notation.meaning: Configuration, planning-coupling, and scheduling-coupling feasible sets.

review_flags: Direct evidence for the complete three-way co-design formulation remains desirable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coupled optimization definition fits the co-design topic and is internally consistent, but the cited generic modeling and network-design sections do not directly support simultaneous planning–scheduling–configuration co-design.

children.title: Planning–Scheduling Coordination Structures
children.top_down_role: Representations of the information exchanged between action-level planning and temporal-resource scheduling.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Integrating Planning and Scheduling; Detecting and Managing Resource Conflicts

children.title: Action-Activity Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Common representations linking selected actions to schedulable activities.

children.title: Shared Action Representations
children.top_down_role: Common planning-side structures used by integrated coordination components.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Action Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One presence variable identifies the same action in planning and scheduling models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\) be a common action index set. For each \(a\in A\), use one Boolean variable \(x_a\) in both the planning constraints and the scheduling constraints. Associate an optional scheduling interval \(I_a\) with presence indicator \(\operatorname{pres}(I_a)\), and impose
\[x_a=\operatorname{pres}(I_a).\]
Planning predicates attach preconditions and effects to \(x_a\); scheduling predicates attach duration, temporal, and resource attributes to \(I_a\). The equality guarantees semantic identity: action \(a\) occurs in the plan if and only if its corresponding scheduled interval is present, eliminating independent action copies that could disagree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common presence variable makes each planning action identical to its optional scheduled interval, synchronizing logical and scheduling interpretations.
assumptions_latex: Planning actions and scheduling intervals share the finite index set \(A\).
Each action has exactly one corresponding optional interval at this representation level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(a\in A\), the planning action is selected if and only if its scheduling interval is present.

notation.meaning: Optional scheduling interval corresponding to action a.

review_flags: The precise shared optional-interval semantics need confirmation from a planning-scheduling representation source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is precise and appropriate for the leaf, but the generic constraint-programming citation does not specifically support identifying a planning-action variable with an optional scheduling-interval presence indicator.

children.title: Shared Activity Representations
children.top_down_role: Common scheduling-side structures used by integrated coordination components.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Activity Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single activity object carries presence, temporal, resource, and planning semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A shared activity representation assigns each activity \(i\) a tuple
\[v_i=(p_i,s_i,e_i,m_i,\rho_i),\]
where \(p_i\in\{0,1\}\) is presence, \(s_i,e_i\) are start and end times, \(m_i\) is an execution mode, and \(\rho_i\) records resource assignments. If \(p_i=1\), the tuple must satisfy \(e_i=s_i+d_i(m_i)\), the planning support and effect conditions associated with activity \(i\), and all temporal and resource constraints. If \(p_i=0\), the activity contributes neither planning effects nor scheduled demand. Thus planning and scheduling constraints reference the same activity object rather than separate linked copies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One activity object jointly stores presence, timing, mode, resources, and planning effects, ensuring both models interpret activity execution consistently.
assumptions_latex: The activity set and every mode domain are finite.
Duration and resource data are defined for each admissible mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Presence \(p_i=1\) simultaneously activates the activity's planning semantics, duration equation, temporal constraints, and resource demands.

notation.meaning: Presence, start, and end of activity i.

review_flags: The tuple is a local formalization; direct integrated activity-representation evidence should be obtained.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tuple gives a coherent shared activity representation and the content kind is appropriate, but it is a local formalization not directly supported by the cited generic constraint-programming section.

children.title: Action-to-Activity Mappings
children.top_down_role: Representational links from selected actions to schedulable activities.

knowledge_statements.title: Action-to-Activity Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sound and complete refinement of planning actions into scheduling activities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a finite action set and \(V\) a finite activity set. An action-to-activity representation is a map \(\phi:A\to 2^V\setminus\{\varnothing\}\) together with channeling constraints \(R_a\) for each \(a\in A\). The constraints \(R_a\) connect the selection, temporal endpoints, effects, and resource requirements of \(a\) to those of \(\phi(a)\). The mapping is sound when every schedule satisfying \(R_a\) realizes the planning semantics of each selected action, and complete when every valid temporal-resource realization of the selected actions extends to values for the activities satisfying all \(R_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mapping refines every planning action into activities and is exact when schedules and valid action realizations correspond in both directions.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(V\) are finite.
Every selected action has at least one associated activity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\) and \(\{R_a:a\in A\}\) form an exact action-activity representation precisely when they are sound and complete.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the proposed sound-and-complete correspondence or specifies the planning semantics, selection variables, and channeling conditions needed to make that correspondence precise.

children.title: Representation Granularity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Mismatches between planning detail and scheduling detail.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Granularity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detects when an activity abstraction is too coarse to preserve scheduling feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a set of detailed activity assignments, let \(F:S\to\{0,1\}\) indicate scheduling feasibility, and let \(\alpha:S\to G\) be a coarser representation. Feasibility is exactly expressible at granularity \(G\) only if \(F\) is constant on every fiber \(\alpha^{-1}(g)\). Consequently, if there exist \(s_1,s_2\in S\) with \(\alpha(s_1)=\alpha(s_2)\) but \(F(s_1)\ne F(s_2)\), then no feasibility predicate depending only on \(g\in G\) can be both sound and complete. Additional ordering, timing, or resource information must be retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abstraction is too coarse whenever it identifies two detailed schedules having different feasibility outcomes.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha\) is a deterministic abstraction map.
\(F\) is the intended detailed feasibility predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(F\) is not constant on a fiber of \(\alpha\), exact feasibility reasoning on \(G\) is impossible.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary formulation is mathematically coherent and matches the granularity leaf, but the nontrivial exact-expressibility claim has no cited source.

children.title: Resource-Conflict Detection Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces exposing scheduling conflicts to planning-level search.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Conflict Detection Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An overload certificate communicated from a cumulative scheduler to planning search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a renewable resource of capacity \(R\). Each mandatory activity \(i\) has duration \(p_i>0\), demand \(r_i>0\), and an execution window contained in \([a,b)\). A resource-conflict interface may return \((U,a,b)\), where \(U\) is a set of mandatory activities satisfying \[\sum_{i\in U}p_i r_i>R(b-a).\] This inequality is a verifiable infeasibility certificate: the required resource energy of \(U\) exceeds the energy available in the interval. The corresponding planning-level flaw identifies the actions mapped to \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface exposes an overloaded activity set and interval whose required resource energy exceeds available capacity.
assumptions_latex: Activities are nonpreemptive and mandatory in the current partial plan.
Each activity in \(U\) must execute entirely within \([a,b)\).
Resource capacity is constant and equal to \(R\) on \([a,b)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in U}p_i r_i>R(b-a)\) certifies infeasibility of the current partial plan.

notation.meaning: duration and resource demand of activity i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the interface leaf, and the overload inequality is valid under the stated containment assumptions, but no inspectable source supports this certificate/interface formulation.

children.title: Resource-Conflict Flaw Management
children.top_down_role: Planning refinements driven by temporal-resource conflicts.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Conflict Flaw Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Planning refinement driven by a sound temporal-resource conflict certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a partial plan \(P
eq\varnothing\), invoke the scheduling layer. If it returns a sound conflict certificate involving activities \(U\), translate \(U\) through the action-activity mapping to a planning flaw \(K\). Generate finitely many refinements \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\) whose disjunction is necessary for resolving \(K\), such as excluding an optional action, changing a resource assignment, or imposing an admissible ordering. Replace \(P\) by the branches \(P_j\) that remain planning-consistent. Repeat until the scheduler reports feasibility or no branch remains; output a feasible refined plan or failure, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scheduling conflicts become planning flaws resolved by a complete set of exclusion, reassignment, or ordering branches.
assumptions_latex: Every returned conflict certificate is sound.
The generated refinements contain every feasible resolution of the reported flaw.
Planning consistency tests never reject a feasible completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a feasible refined plan or exhausts all refinements represented by its branching scheme.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits flaw management, but no source supports completeness, and finite branching at each iteration alone does not ensure termination or exhaustive search without a finite refinement space, progress condition, or duplicate-state control.

children.title: Hybrid Solver Architectures
children.top_down_role: Computational organizations assigning coupled structures to specialized reasoning engines.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Incorporating OR into CP; Toward Integration of CP and OR

children.title: CP-SAT Lazy-Clause Architecture Family
children.top_down_role: Integration of propagation, nogood learning, and Boolean search.

children.title: CP–SAT Integration
children.top_down_role: Combined constraint propagation and Boolean search within integrated solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: CP–SAT Integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Channeling finite-domain constraints into a clause-learning Boolean search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-domain variables constrained by \(C\), and let \(B\) contain Boolean literals encoding domain facts such as \(x=v\) or \(x\le v\). A CP–SAT integration consists of channeling constraints between \(X\) and \(B\), a SAT engine maintaining a Boolean trail, and CP propagators for \(C\). Every propagated literal or detected inconsistency must admit an entailed clausal explanation. A total Boolean assignment represents a solution exactly when it is encoding-consistent and its decoded values satisfy \(C\). Thus Boolean learning remains sound while specialized propagators enforce nonclausal constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-domain facts are Boolean-encoded, while CP propagators provide explained deductions and SAT manages search and learning.
assumptions_latex: Every variable domain is finite.
The Boolean encoding is consistent and decodable.
Every imported explanation is entailed by the encoded model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Satisfying decoded assignments are exactly the solutions of \(C\), and learned clauses preserve them.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is suitable for the integration leaf, but no source establishes the asserted exact encoding/decoding correspondence and explanation requirements.

children.title: Lazy-Clause Generation Architectures
children.top_down_role: Architectures that expose propagation explanations as learned clauses.

knowledge_statements.title: Lazy-Clause Generation Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A lazy-clause-generation search loop with explained CP propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a Boolean trail with the root-level encoding clauses. Repeatedly apply SAT unit propagation and CP propagation to a fixpoint. Each CP deduction \(\ell\) is accompanied by an explanation clause entailing \(\ell\). If a conflict occurs, resolve its explanation with trail reasons, learn an asserting clause, and backjump to the computed decision level. If propagation is consistent but the assignment is incomplete, choose an unassigned literal and open a decision level. Return the decoded assignment when all constraints are satisfied; return infeasible when conflict analysis derives the empty clause at the root level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solver alternates Boolean and CP propagation, learns clauses from explained conflicts, backjumps, and branches until solution or root contradiction.
assumptions_latex: All finite-domain literals have a sound Boolean encoding.
Every CP deduction and conflict has an entailed explanation clause.
Branching eventually assigns every required decision literal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs a satisfying decoded assignment or derives root-level infeasibility.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits lazy-clause generation, but no source is cited, and the stated branching condition does not by itself specify all finiteness and fairness conditions needed for the solution-or-infeasibility conclusion.

children.title: Propagation-to-Clause Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Interfaces connecting propagator explanations to clause learning.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation-to-Clause Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clausal explanations certifying CP propagations and conflicts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the encoded model and \(A\) the current consistent set of trail literals. A propagation-to-clause interface certifies a propagated literal \(\ell\) by returning \(E\subseteq A\) such that \(F\land\bigwedge E\models\ell\). The interface exports the clause \[\bigvee_{e\in E}\neg e\;\lor\;\ell,\] which is entailed by \(F\) and becomes unit under \(E\). For a conflict it returns \(E\subseteq A\) satisfying \(F\land\bigwedge E\models\bot\), thereby exporting the entailed conflict clause \(\bigvee_{e\in E}\neg e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A CP propagator exports an entailed clause explaining either its deduction or the inconsistency it detects.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) consists of literals currently true on the Boolean trail.
The propagator reasons soundly with respect to \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exported reason or conflict clause is entailed by \(F\) and is valid for clause learning.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind accurately fits propagation-to-clause interfaces, and the formulas are internally consistent, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the explanation-clause specification.

children.title: Boolean Search Coordination
children.top_down_role: Coordination of Boolean branching with domain-specific propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Search Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordination of decisions, propagation, learning, and backjumping through one Boolean trail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a single Boolean trail \(T\) partitioned into decision levels. At each iteration, perform unit propagation and request all registered theory propagators to extend \(T\) with explained literals until a fixpoint is reached. On conflict, analyze the supplied explanation, learn an asserting clause, erase assignments above its backjump level, and resume propagation. When no conflict exists, branch on an unassigned literal unless the decoded assignment is complete. Output the decoded solution when complete; output infeasible if the empty clause is derived at decision level zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One Boolean trail coordinates branching, theory propagation, clause learning, backjumping, and termination.
assumptions_latex: Every theory contribution has an entailed clausal explanation.
The branching rule is exhaustive over the finite encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinated search returns a decoded solution or a root-level contradiction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits Boolean search coordination, but no source supports the architecture, and exhaustive finite branching alone does not fully state the progress and propagation-termination conditions required by the conclusion.

children.title: CP–MIP Hybrid Architectures
children.top_down_role: Cooperation between discrete propagation and mathematical-programming relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: CP–MIP Hybrid Architectures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cooperation between finite-domain propagation and valid mathematical-programming relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given discrete variables \(X\), constraints \(C\), and a mixed-integer relaxation \(M\), initialize shared bounds and channeling constraints. Repeatedly apply CP propagation to \(C\), transfer tightened bounds to \(M\), solve the current relaxation, and return only globally valid bounds or cuts to the CP layer. If either layer proves inconsistency, backtrack or prune the synchronized node. Otherwise branch on a shared variable and communicate the branch to both layers. For optimization, retain every feasible incumbent and stop when all nodes are pruned or the global relaxation bound meets the incumbent value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CP domain filtering and MIP relaxation bounds cooperate through synchronized variables, valid cuts, branching, and incumbents.
assumptions_latex: The CP model and MIP relaxation use sound channeling constraints.
Every imported cut is valid for all feasible solutions represented at its scope.
Optimization bounds use a consistent objective convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hybrid search preserves feasible solutions and terminates with infeasibility or a certified optimal incumbent after complete node exhaustion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm describes a plausible CP–MIP hybrid, but no source is cited and the assumptions do not guarantee finite node exhaustion or attainment of a certified optimum, particularly when the relaxation contains continuous variables.

children.title: Master–Subproblem Coordination
children.top_down_role: Separation of strategic choices from temporal, resource, or configuration feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Master–Subproblem Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logic-based decomposition of strategic decisions from detailed feasibility and cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in Y\) denote master decisions and let \(Q(y)\) be the optimum of a temporal-resource-configuration subproblem. Solve a master relaxation for \(y^k\), then evaluate the subproblem. If it is infeasible, add a valid feasibility constraint excluding \(y^k\) and every other master assignment covered by its conflict certificate. If it is feasible with value \(Q(y^k)\), update the incumbent and add a valid lower estimator \(\theta\ge L_k(y)\) satisfying \(L_k(y)\le Q(y)\). Repeat until the master lower bound is no smaller than the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master proposes strategic choices; a detailed subproblem returns feasibility conflicts or valid cost estimators until the bound closes.
assumptions_latex: The master domain \(Y\) is finite or otherwise solved to the required global guarantees.
Every feasibility constraint and lower estimator is globally valid.
Each subproblem is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, the incumbent minimizes the integrated objective over all feasible master and subproblem decisions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits master–subproblem coordination, but no source supports it. The integrated objective and master contribution are not defined, Q(y) is used both as a value and as infeasibility, and validity of cuts alone does not guarantee finite convergence.

children.title: Cooperative Solver Portfolio Family
children.top_down_role: Multiple encodings or solvers exchanging bounds, conflicts, incumbents, or subproblem information.

children.title: Solver Portfolio Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection or scheduling of complementary solver configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver Portfolio Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feature-based selection of a solver under a stated resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S\) be a finite solver portfolio, \(z(I)\) the feature vector of instance \(I\), \(B>0\) a resource budget, and \(\widehat L(s,z,B)\) a predicted loss. Select \[s^*(I)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in\mathcal S}\widehat L\bigl(s,z(I),B\bigr),\] using a fixed deterministic tie rule. Run \(s^*(I)\) for at most \(B\) units of the declared resource and return its certified solution, bound, or status. The loss definition must specify how timeout, infeasibility, objective quality, and runtime are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Instance features and a declared loss model select one portfolio solver to run within a fixed resource budget.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) is finite and nonempty.
\(z(I)\) is available before solver selection.
\(\widehat L\) assigns a comparable real loss to every candidate solver.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s^*(I)\) minimizes predicted loss within the stated portfolio and budget model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is precise and fits solver portfolio selection, but the cited section concerns financial portfolio selection in a nonlinear-integer-programming applications chapter, not algorithm selection among solvers. A source on algorithm or solver portfolio selection is required.

children.title: Cooperative Solver Exchange
children.top_down_role: Information exchange among concurrently or sequentially cooperating solvers.

knowledge_statements.title: Cooperative Solver Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound exchange of bounds, incumbents, and conflicts among heterogeneous solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run solvers \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\) on a common model \(F\). Each solver may publish a message consisting of a feasible incumbent, a globally valid objective bound, or a constraint entailed by \(F\). Before importing a message, a recipient verifies model identity, variable mapping, objective convention, and message scope. Valid incumbents tighten the shared cutoff, bounds permit only justified pruning, and entailed constraints may strengthen local propagation. Stop when a solver supplies a checkable terminal certificate, the shared optimality gap closes, or the resource budget is exhausted; return the best certified common status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heterogeneous solvers exchange only compatible, verifiable incumbents, bounds, and entailed conflicts through a shared model interface.
assumptions_latex: All solvers address the same feasible set and objective after channeling.
Every imported message is sound at its declared scope.
Shared updates are applied monotonically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cooperation preserves every feasible solution and may strengthen bounds or propagation without invalidating terminal certificates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits cooperative solver exchange, but no source supports the protocol. The meaning of a checkable terminal certificate and the aggregation rule for the best common status require specification before the conclusion is reliable.

children.title: Bound Sharing Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Exchange of objective bounds across solver components.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound Sharing Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention; maximization uses reversed inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound-sharing interface is a protocol that transmits a tuple \((R,L_R,\sigma)\), where \(R\subseteq X\), \(L_R\le \inf\{f(x):x\in R\cap F\}\), and \(\sigma\) identifies the model version, search-region definition, and assumptions under which the bound is valid. A receiver may combine bounds having identical compatible scope by replacing its lower bound on \(R\) with their maximum. Given a feasible-incumbent value \(U\), it may discard \(R\) when \(L_R\ge U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound-sharing interface exchanges valid region-specific lower bounds together with their model and assumption scope, allowing compatible solvers to strengthen bounds and safely prune regions dominated by a feasible incumbent.
assumptions_latex: The global problem is \(\inf\{f(x):x\in F\}\), where \(X\) is the decision space, \(F\subseteq X\) is the feasible set, and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
Every exported bound is valid for the explicitly identified search region, model version, and assumption scope.
The incumbent value \(U\) is the objective value of a feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For a compatible imported bound \(L_R\), pruning \(R\) when \(L_R\ge U\) removes no feasible solution having objective value strictly less than \(U\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the global minimization problem.
Objective value of the best shared feasible incumbent.
Valid lower bound for search region R under the recorded scope.
Identified subset of the global search space.
Model-version, region-definition, and assumption-scope metadata for the bound.

children.title: Conflict Sharing Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Exchange of learned conflicts across encodings or solvers.

assumptions_latex: All solvers interpret the shared variables and literals through a common model mapping.
An exported conflict is logically implied by the current model version.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adding the shared constraint \(\neg C\), or an equivalent consequence, preserves every feasible solution of the common model.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the common integrated model.
Conjunction of assignments or literals forming the rejected partial decision.
Logical entailment under the common model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers shared nogoods, clauses, and valid domain cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A conflict-sharing interface exports a tuple \((C,V,\pi)\), where \(C\) is a conjunction of mapped decisions, \(V\) is the model version, and \(\pi\) records a validation basis such that \(F_V\models
eg C\). The receiver accepts the conflict only if its variable mapping and active assumptions are compatible with \(V\). It may then add \(
eg C\), or any consequence \(D\) satisfying \(F_V\models D\) and \(D\models
eg C\), as a pruning constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conflict interface exchanges model-implied nogoods with variable mappings and validity metadata, so receiving solvers can reject incompatible partial decisions without excluding feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Conflict Sharing Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local topic fit, but the cited domain-cut section does not establish the proposed conflict-transfer tuple, compatibility contract, or validation metadata. The use of F_V also requires an explicit definition tied to V before this formulation can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Incumbent Sharing Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Exchange of candidate solutions and associated quality information.

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Sharing Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incumbents must include every cross-domain decision required for feasibility checking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An incumbent-sharing interface transmits \((x,f(x),V,\rho)\), where \(V\) identifies a model version, \(x\in X\) assigns every required planning, scheduling, configuration, and policy variable, and \(\rho\) contains the data needed to check \(x\in F_V\). A receiver accepts the tuple only after validating its model compatibility and the membership \(x\in F_V\). It then updates \(U\leftarrow\min\{U,f(x)\}\) and may use the resulting feasible-incumbent value in sound bound-based pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incumbent-sharing interface exchanges complete cross-domain solutions with objective values, model identity, and feasibility-validation data, enabling compatible solvers to improve their incumbent and prune regions using valid bounds.
assumptions_latex: For each compatible model version \(V\), the integrated minimization problem is \(\inf\{f(x):x\in F_V\}\), where \(F_V\subseteq X\) and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
The sender and receiver share a compatibility test for model versions and complete assignments.
Only an assignment verified to lie in \(F_V\) is accepted as an incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(x\in F_V\) is accepted, then \(U_{\mathrm{new}}=\min\{U_{\mathrm{old}},f(x)\}\) is a feasible-incumbent value, and any region having a valid lower bound at least \(U_{\mathrm{new}}\) contains no strictly improving feasible solution.

notation.meaning: Feasible set for model version V.
Objective function of the integrated minimization problem.
Identifier of the model version under which feasibility is checked.
Payload supporting compatibility and feasibility validation.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

children.title: Cross-Domain Assurance-Repair System
children.top_down_role: Artifacts supporting validation, failure localization, and repair across planning, scheduling, and configuration boundaries.

children.title: Cross-Domain Feasibility Witnesses
children.top_down_role: Composite plans, schedules, configurations, and execution policies supporting feasibility.

assumptions_latex: The integrated constraint system is \(F=F_P\cap F_S\cap F_C\cap F_E\) over a common assignment space.
Every interface variable shared by two domains has one consistent value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful verification of all component and coupling predicates certifies \(w\in F\).

notation.meaning: Composite plan, schedule, configuration, and execution-policy assignment.
Feasible set of the integrated model.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directly checkable witness for integrated feasibility, not merely separate domain feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cross-domain feasibility witness is a tuple \(w=(p,s,c,e)\) together with shared-variable values such that \(p\in F_P\), \(s\in F_S\), \(c\in F_C\), \(e\in F_E\), and every coupling predicate in \(G\) evaluates to true. Its verifier checks the four domain predicates, equality of duplicated interface variables, and all constraints in \(G\). Acceptance certifies \(w\in F_P\cap F_S\cap F_C\cap F_E\cap G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasibility witness combines a plan, schedule, configuration, and execution policy whose domain constraints, shared variables, and cross-domain coupling constraints all verify.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Domain Feasibility Witnesses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A certificate is an appropriate knowledge kind, but the assumptions define F as the intersection of four domain sets while the statement separately intersects with G and then identifies that larger intersection with F. The generic constraint-programming citation does not support the proposed composite certificate or verifier.

children.title: Cross-Domain Conflict Explanations
children.top_down_role: Conflicts spanning action choice, timing, resources, components, and requirements.

assumptions_latex: The integrated model has feasible set \(F\) over decision space \(X\).
The explanation predicate is expressed through mapped decisions from at least two coupled domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The entailment \(F\models\neg C\) certifies that no globally feasible solution extends all decisions in \(C\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the integrated model.
A checkable derivation of the conflict entailment.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a conflict explanation is a checkable cross-domain nogood implied by the integrated constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The explanation must span at least two of planning, timing, resources, configuration, or requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cross-domain conflict explanation is a pair \((C,\pi)\), where \(C= igwedge_{i\in I}d_i\) contains mapped decisions from at least two coupled domains and \(\pi\) is verifiable evidence that \(F\models
eg C\). The explanation is irreducible when \(F
ot\models
eg igwedge_{i\in I\setminus\{j\}}d_i\) for every \(j\in I\). Irreducibility is optional; validity requires only the first entailment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cross-domain conflict explanation is a verifiable nogood involving decisions from multiple domains; removing any decision yields an irreducible explanation when that stronger property holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Domain Conflict Explanations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role is plausible and the entailment formulation is coherent, but no inspectable source supports either the cross-domain explanation definition or its deletion-based irreducibility condition.

children.title: Cross-Domain Decomposition Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Bounds and infeasible-subproblem artifacts exchanged by hybrid methods.

children.title: Cross-Domain Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Artifacts supporting bounds that depend on multiple integrated domains.

assumptions_latex: The integrated problem minimizes \(f(x)\) over \(x\in F\).
Each component bound is valid under the interface assignment and model version named by the certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A verified certificate proves \(L\le z^*\), where \(z^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Interface assignments or multipliers coupling domain bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound certificate for minimization; upper-bound certificates follow by sign reversal.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Continuous bound versus Lagrangian bound p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cross-domain bound certificate is data \((y,L_1,\ldots,L_m,\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_m)\) whose verifier establishes valid domain or relaxation inequalities under common interface data \(y\), and a composition rule \(L=\Phi(L_1,\ldots,L_m,y)\). The rule must satisfy \(L\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). Consequently, after checking interface consistency, every \(\pi_i\), and the computation of \(\Phi\), the receiver certifies \(L\le z^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cross-domain bound certificate combines verifiable domain bounds under consistent interface data through a sound rule, producing a certified bound on the integrated optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Domain Bound Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.3 Continuous bound versus Lagrangian bound p. 26

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the leaf, but the cited comparison of continuous and Lagrangian bounds does not support the general cross-domain certificate structure or the arbitrary composition map Phi. A decomposition or proof-certificate source specifying a sound composition rule is required.

children.title: Infeasible-Subproblem Certificates
children.top_down_role: Artifacts identifying infeasibility within a delegated hybrid subproblem.

assumptions_latex: Fix an interface assignment \(y\) and model version \(V\).
The subproblem feasible set is \(F_k(y,V)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Verifier acceptance certifies \(F_k(y,V)=\varnothing\), so any global assignment inducing \(y\) is infeasible unless the certificate scope is changed.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of subproblem k under interface data and model version.
Interface assignment fixed by the coordinating problem.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract verifier form covering contradictory cores, dual rays, and exhaustive finite-domain refutations.

source_refs.locator: 6.2 Decision Problems, and Classes NP and P p. 96

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An infeasible-subproblem certificate is a tuple \((k,y,V,\pi)\) accepted by a deterministic verifier only if \(\pi\) establishes \(F_k(y,V)=\varnothing\). The evidence may be an inconsistent constraint core, a valid dual ray, or a complete finite-domain refutation, according to the subproblem class. The tuple must delimit every assumption used by \(\pi\); therefore its conclusion applies only to global candidates whose projection induces the same scoped interface conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible-subproblem certificate provides checkable evidence that a named subproblem has no solution under specified interface data, assumptions, and model version.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.2 Decision Problems, and Classes NP and P p. 96

The conclusion about every global assignment inducing y also requires an explicit relation between global feasibility and the named subproblem.

children.title: Certificate Exchange Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Transfer of certificate artifacts between master and subproblem components.

assumptions_latex: Each solver exposes a deterministic certificate verifier.
Producer and consumer agree on identifiers for variables, constraints, domains, and model versions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only a certificate satisfying \(\operatorname{Verify}(V,T)=1\) may soundly update the receiving solver's bounds, conflicts, or feasibility state.
