knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic contract for exchanging feasibility, infeasibility, and bound certificates among heterogeneous solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A certificate exchange interface defines a typed transfer object \(T=(\tau,V,S,P,\pi)\), where \(\tau\) is the certificate kind, \(V\) is the model version, \(S\) is its assumption scope, \(P\) is its mathematical payload, and \(\pi\) is checkable evidence. Import is permitted exactly when identifiers resolve, the active assumptions contain \(S\), and \(\operatorname{Verify}(V,T)=1\). Rejected or unverifiable objects have no pruning or certification effect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate exchange interface specifies certificate type, model version, scope, payload, evidence, identifier mapping, and a receiver-side acceptance rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Exchange Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is suitable for this interface leaf, but no source supports the transfer schema or its exact import rule. The condition that active assumptions 'contain' S also needs a formally specified direction of assumption compatibility.

children.title: Certificate Provenance
children.top_down_role: Links from exchanged certificates to responsible subproblems, bounds, and source decisions.

assumptions_latex: Certificate and model objects have stable identifiers.
The provenance graph is append-only and every derivation rule has a deterministic checker.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every ancestor of \(c\) is available and every derivation edge verifies, the certificate \(c\) can be independently reconstructed or revalidated.

notation.meaning: Certificate node whose origin is recorded.
Derivation relation from parent artifacts to a result.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: provenance is represented by immutable dependency records linking artifacts, assumptions, transformations, and results
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Append-only derivation provenance for independently checking certificate origin and validity scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Certificate provenance is represented by a directed acyclic graph \(G=(N,E)\). Each node records an immutable artifact identifier, content digest, producer, model version, assumption scope, and creation order. An edge \((A,r,c)\in E\) asserts that certificate \(c\) was obtained from parent set \(A\subseteq N\) by rule \(r\). Valid provenance requires every parent to precede \(c\), every digest to match its artifact, and the checker for \(r\) to validate the recorded derivation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate provenance is an append-only acyclic graph linking each certificate to immutable inputs, assumptions, model version, producer, derivation rule, and content digest.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Provenance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the proposed mandatory DAG fields and validation rules lack a source. Verified provenance edges can support revalidation, yet independent reconstruction additionally requires available artifacts and executable reconstruction rules, which the statement does not require.

children.title: Repair Decision Provenance System
children.top_down_role: Traceable relationships among disruptions, conflicts, revised decisions, and resulting repairs.

children.title: Integrated Repair Artifacts
children.top_down_role: Cross-domain revisions produced in response to integrated conflicts or disruptions.

assumptions_latex: An original integrated solution \(x^0\) and disrupted model version \(V^1\) are given.
The repair model identifies mutable decisions and a disruption cost \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Verifier acceptance certifies feasibility of \(x^1\) for \(V^1\) and confirms that its recorded changes and objective values match the artifact.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: an integrated repair artifact must package the repaired assignment with deltas, validation evidence, and decision lineage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite artifact joining repaired decisions, validation evidence, and recorded deviations from the pre-disruption solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integrated repair artifact is a tuple \((V^0,V^1,x^0,x^1,D,q,\pi)\), where \(D=\{i:x_i^0\ne x_i^1\}\), \(q\) records objective and disruption values, and \(\pi\) supports verification that \(x^1\in F_{V^1}\). Its checker recomputes \(D\), verifies every planning, scheduling, configuration, and policy constraint, checks shared-variable consistency, and confirms the recorded value \(\Delta(x^0,x^1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrated repair artifact packages the old and repaired solutions, changed decisions, objective and disruption values, model versions, and cross-domain feasibility evidence.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrated Repair Artifacts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A certificate-like repair artifact is plausible for the leaf, but the exact tuple, mandatory checker behavior, and cross-domain scope have no cited support. The component q is also introduced only informally and its required objective values are not specified.

children.title: Decision Traceability
children.top_down_role: Traceable links among original, revised, and retained decisions.

assumptions_latex: Decision, constraint, observation, and artifact identifiers are stable within each model version.
Every derived decision records the rule and parent records used to derive it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every reported decision \(d\), reachability in \(G\) identifies its supporting inputs and every downstream artifact affected by changing \(d\).

notation.meaning: Directed reachability relation in the provenance graph.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bidirectional traceability is graph reachability between decisions and their supporting or dependent records
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional traceability between repair decisions, their causes, and their downstream consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A repair record has decision traceability when its provenance graph \(G=(N,E)\) satisfies two conditions for every decision node \(d\). First, some recorded requirement, disruption, conflict, or prior decision \(a\) satisfies \(a\leadsto_G d\). Second, every reported outcome or certificate that depends on \(d\) is reachable from \(d\). Each edge stores a typed derivation relation and model version, so both upstream justification and downstream impact are mechanically queryable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision traceability requires graph paths from each repair decision to its recorded causes and to every outcome or certificate that depends on it.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision Traceability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits, but no source supports the proposed bidirectional reachability criterion. Graph reachability records declared dependency; by itself it does not establish that changing d actually affects every reachable artifact, and requiring every decision to have a prior cause may improperly exclude root decisions.

children.title: Disruption-to-Decision Links
children.top_down_role: Connections from operational disruptions to affected planning, scheduling, or configuration decisions.

assumptions_latex: The baseline model is \(V^0\), and the disrupted model is \(V^1\).
Each repair decision has a stable identifier and a recorded justification predicate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A link \((\delta,d,\pi)\) is valid only when replay verifies that \(d\) responds to \(\delta\) under the recorded model transition.

notation.meaning: Recorded disruption event or model delta.
Repair decision attributed to the disruption.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a disruption-to-decision link is a typed, versioned attribution edge with replayable evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Typed causal-attribution records, distinct from mere temporal ordering of disruptions and decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A disruption-to-decision link is a record \((\delta,d,V^0,V^1,	au,\pi)\), where \(\delta\) is a model or observation change, \(d\) is a repair decision, \(\tau\) names the attribution type, and \(\pi\) is replayable evidence. The link is valid when the recorded transition from \(V^0\) to \(V^1\) contains \(\delta\), decision \(d\) satisfies its declared response predicate, and the checker for \(\tau\) accepts \(\pi\). Temporal succession alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disruption-to-decision link records a typed, versioned, and verifiable attribution from a disruption to a repair decision; temporal order alone does not establish the link.
knowledge_statements.title: Disruption-to-Decision Links

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the link-oriented leaf, but no source supports the exact record or its claimed causal validity. A self-declared response predicate and checker acceptance do not by themselves establish attribution without externally specified semantics for each link type.

children.title: Conflict-to-Repair Links
children.top_down_role: Connections from diagnosed conflicts to the repairs chosen to address them.

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-to-Repair Links
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A trace relation connecting detected conflicts to the repair decisions intended to resolve them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be detected conflicts and \(R\) be repair decisions. A conflict-to-repair representation is a relation \(L\subseteq C\times R\) with annotations \(w(c,r)=(D_{c,r},V_{c,r})\), where \(D_{c,r}\) identifies the commitments changed by \(r\) because of \(c\), and \(V_{c,r}\) is a post-repair validation predicate. A link \((c,r)\in L\) is resolved exactly when executing \(r\) produces state \(x_r\) satisfying \(V_{c,r}(x_r)=1\). Every claimed resolution must have at least one such link and retain the conflict identifier, repair identifier, changed commitments, and validation result.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each claimed conflict resolution links the conflict to a repair, identifies the affected commitments, and records a post-repair validation result.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) and \(R\) have stable identifiers.
Every executed repair has an observable post-repair state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((c,r)\in L\) and \(V_{c,r}(x_r)=1\) provide the conflict-to-repair trace for a claimed resolution.

notation.meaning: Commitments changed by the linked repair.

children.title: Repair Outcome Provenance
children.top_down_role: Records connecting revised decisions to resulting feasibility and operational outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Repair Outcome Provenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A verifiable record of the state transition and validation produced by an executed repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an executed repair \(r\), a repair-outcome provenance certificate is the tuple \(P_r=(x^{-},r,x^{+},Q,
u)\), where \(x^{-}\) and \(x^{+}\) are the recorded pre-repair and post-repair states, \(Q=(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\) is a declared validation suite, and \(\nu_i=q_i(x^{+})\). The certificate supports a successful outcome claim only if replaying \(r\) from \(x^{-}\) yields \(x^{+}\), every required validation has \(\nu_i=1\), and the record preserves the versions of the model, data, and repair parameters used in replay.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outcome provenance records the before-state, repair, after-state, validation results, and versions needed to replay and check a successful repair.
assumptions_latex: Repair execution is reproducible under recorded model, data, and parameter versions.
Each required validation predicate returns a Boolean result.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_r\) certifies success only when replay and all required validation checks agree with its recorded outcome.

notation.meaning: Recorded states before and after repair.

children.title: Integrated Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Characteristic failures caused by mismatched abstractions, weak coordination, or execution change.

children.title: Feasible Plans with Infeasible Schedules
children.top_down_role: Action-level feasibility lost after timing or resource commitments are introduced.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Plans with Infeasible Schedules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Untimed action feasibility does not imply feasibility after durations, resources, and deadlines are imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) be an action sequence that reaches the goal under an untimed transition model. Its scheduling extension is feasible only if start times \(s_i\) satisfy all precedence, duration, resource, release, and deadline constraints. The implication from plan feasibility to schedule feasibility fails when this timing system has no solution. Concretely, two actions of duration one may form an untimed feasible plan, yet if both require one unary resource and both must finish by time one, no nonoverlapping start times can satisfy the deadline. Thus action-level reachability alone cannot certify integrated feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid untimed action sequence can become unschedulable when durations, shared resources, or deadlines are added; two unit tasks on one resource before time one suffice.
assumptions_latex: The planning model omits at least one timing or resource restriction enforced by the scheduling model.
Scheduled actions are nonpreemptive in the concrete example.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Plan feasibility does not imply existence of start times satisfying the integrated scheduling constraints.

notation.meaning: Start time assigned to action i.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role matches the container and the example is standard, but no source is supplied and the concrete example does not explicitly state the start-time domain or nonnegative time origin needed for its deadline contradiction.

children.title: Valid Configurations with Inoperable Plans
children.top_down_role: Structurally valid products lacking operational capability for required plans.

knowledge_statements.title: Valid Configurations with Inoperable Plans
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural configuration validity does not ensure that required operational goals are achievable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be configurations satisfying structural constraints \(G(k)=1\), and let \(A(k)\) be the actions enabled by configuration \(k\). A valid configuration \(k\in K\) is inoperable for initial state \(x_0\) and goal set \(T\) when no finite sequence over \(A(k)\) reaches \(T\). In particular, if every goal-reaching sequence requires capability \(q\), while structural validity permits a configuration \(k\) with \(q\notin A(k)\), then \(G(k)=1\) but the induced planning problem is infeasible. Structural consistency therefore does not certify operational adequacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product may satisfy every structural configuration rule yet enable no plan for a required goal because it lacks a necessary operational capability.
assumptions_latex: Configuration validity and operational reachability are modeled by distinct constraint families.
Enabled actions are determined by the selected configuration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(k)=1\) need not imply that a goal-reaching plan exists under \(A(k)\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed failure regime fits the container, but the statement compares capability q directly with the action set A(k), leaving their types inconsistent. A source and a typed capability-to-action enabling model are needed before fixing the formulation.

children.title: Encoding Fidelity Gap Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Weak or oversized encodings caused by lost structure, coarse bounds, or unsuitable horizons.

children.title: Relaxation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Weak surrogate models whose bounds poorly reflect the integrated problem.

assumptions_latex: \(\varnothing\neq F\subseteq R\subseteq X\).
The optimal values \(z_F\) and \(z_R\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=z_F-z_R\geq 0\), and \(g>0\) implies that the relaxation is not objective-exact for \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective and feasibility discrepancies created by replacing an integrated feasible set with a relaxation.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with nonempty feasible set \(F\subseteq X\), objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and relaxation \(F\subseteq R\subseteq X\), suppose the values \(z_F=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\) and \(z_R=\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\) are finite. The absolute relaxation gap is \(g=z_F-z_R\geq 0\). When \(z_F\neq 0\), a relative gap may be reported as \(g_{\mathrm{rel}}=(z_F-z_R)/|z_F|\). A positive gap means that the relaxed bound is strictly below the integrated optimum. Independently, any point in \(R\setminus F\) witnesses that the relaxation admits a point infeasible for the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite optimal values, a relaxation gap measures how much the relaxed optimum understates the true minimization optimum; relaxed points outside the original feasible set separately witness lost feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Gaps

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Compilation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Loss of useful structure during translation into a solver representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Compilation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of soundness or completeness when one domain model is compiled into another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be source-model solutions, \(T\) compiled-model solutions, \(E:S\to Y\) an encoding, and \(D:T\to X\) a decoding. A compilation is feasibility exact when every \(s\in S\) has some \(t\in T\) representing \(E(s)\), and every \(t\in T\) decodes to \(D(t)\in S\). A compilation gap occurs if completeness fails, so a source-feasible solution has no compiled representative, or soundness fails, so a compiled-feasible solution decodes to a source-infeasible object. Objective fidelity additionally fails when corresponding solutions have unequal declared costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compilation gap exists when translation loses a valid source solution, admits a spurious compiled solution, or changes the cost of corresponding solutions.
assumptions_latex: Source and compiled feasibility semantics are explicitly defined.
Encoding and decoding identify which solutions are intended to correspond.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of soundness, completeness, or preserved objective value constitutes a compilation gap.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but E maps source solutions into Y while compiled representatives lie in T, and no relation between Y and T is defined. Consequently the completeness condition is not mathematically well formed. A source-backed correspondence model is required.

children.title: Structural Information Loss
children.top_down_role: Encoding choices that obscure exploitable planning, scheduling, or configuration structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Information Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An abstraction loses structure when it merges states requiring different feasibility or repair decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be detailed integrated states, \(Y\) an abstract representation, and \(\alpha:X\to Y\) the abstraction map. For a decision-relevant predicate \(P:X\to\{0,1\}\), structural information loss occurs exactly when there exist \(x_1,x_2\in X\) such that \(\alpha(x_1)=\alpha(x_2)\) but \(P(x_1)\neq P(x_2)\). More generally, for a required repair map \(R:X\rightrightarrows U\), loss occurs when equal abstractions have distinct admissible-repair sets. No decision rule depending only on \(\alpha(x)\) can then reproduce the detailed predicate or repair set for every state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abstraction loses decision-relevant structure when it maps two detailed states together even though their feasibility classifications or admissible repairs differ.
assumptions_latex: The predicate or repair correspondence is evaluated on detailed states.
Downstream decisions observe only the abstract representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equal abstract images with unequal detailed decisions make exact abstract recovery impossible.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The predicate-based information-loss condition is coherent and matches the leaf, but the extension to admissible repair sets depends on whether exact set recovery or merely selection of a valid repair is required. No source establishes the intended semantics.

children.title: Coarse-Bound Weakness
children.top_down_role: Poor search guidance caused by bounds that are insufficiently discriminating.

assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
The regional optimum \(z_N\) is finite, \(L_N\leq z_N\) is a valid lower bound, and \(U\) is the value of a feasible incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L_N<U\leq z_N\), bound validity holds, but the usual bound test cannot prune region \(N\).

notation.meaning: True optimum within search region N.
Additive weakness of the regional lower bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A valid but loose node bound provides little pruning or coordination information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimization over a search region \(F_N\) having finite regional optimum \(z_N\), a valid lower bound \(L_N\leq z_N\), and a feasible incumbent value \(U\). The additive weakness of the regional bound is \(w_N=z_N-L_N\geq 0\). The usual bound test can certify that region \(N\) cannot improve the incumbent when \(L_N\geq U\). Thus, if \(L_N<U\leq z_N\), the lower bound is valid but cannot prune a region whose true optimum cannot improve the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coarse lower bound is valid but fails the usual pruning test when it lies below the incumbent even though the region's true optimum cannot improve that incumbent.
knowledge_statements.title: Coarse-Bound Weakness

children.title: Horizon Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Encoding degradation caused by unsuitable temporal or decision horizons.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite planning or scheduling horizon fails to preserve feasibility of the required operational interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the integrated model require constraints on times \([0,T]\), while a component model is solved only on \([0,H]\). If \(H<T\), horizon mismatch occurs when a component-feasible prefix has no feasible extension to \([0,T]\), or when a globally feasible solution is excluded by an artificial terminal condition at \(H\). For example, a prefix may defer mandatory maintenance until after \(H\), although resource or deadline constraints make that maintenance impossible before \(T\). Feasibility on the truncated horizon therefore neither guarantees extendability nor, under restrictive terminal conditions, preserves every global solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A truncated horizon can accept prefixes that cannot be completed or reject globally feasible solutions through an artificial terminal condition.
assumptions_latex: The required operational interval ends at \(T\).
At least one component is optimized on a horizon ending at \(H<T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Truncated-horizon feasibility is not equivalent to feasibility over \([0,T]\) without an exact extension condition.

notation.meaning: End of the required operational interval.
End of the truncated component horizon.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two horizon-mismatch phenomena fit the failure-boundary container, but no source supports the exact formulation, particularly the conditions under which a terminal constraint at H excludes a globally feasible continuation.

children.title: Decomposition Coordination Failure
children.top_down_role: Slow or unstable coordination caused by weak cross-block information or tight coupling.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Coordination Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blockwise feasible iterates fail to achieve or stably approach cross-block consistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition an integrated decision vector as \(x=(x^1,\ldots,x^m)\), and express cross-block consistency by residual \(r(x)\), with coordination achieved exactly when \(r(x)=0\). For decomposition iterates \(x_k\), coordination failure occurs if the method terminates with \(\|r(x_k)\|>\varepsilon\), or if it generates infinitely many iterates with \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|r(x_k)\|>\varepsilon\) for a prescribed tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). Persistent cycling among incompatible block solutions is a special case. Individual block feasibility does not prevent this failure because the violated conditions couple multiple blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decomposition coordination fails when locally feasible blocks terminate, cycle, or persist without satisfying the shared coupling constraints to the required tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Each block subproblem has a defined local feasible set.
A residual measures all required cross-block consistency conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local block feasibility does not imply integrated feasibility when the coordination residual remains above \(\varepsilon\).

children.title: Cross-Domain Operational Instability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Local changes propagating across plans, schedules, configurations, and commitments.

children.title: Repair Cascades
children.top_down_role: Local repairs that trigger further revisions across integrated domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Repair Cascades
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The transitive propagation of one repair through coupled planning, scheduling, and configuration commitments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a directed dependency graph of commitments, and let \(S_0\subseteq V\) be commitments directly changed by an initial repair. Define \(S_{j+1}=S_j\cup\{v\in V:\exists u\in S_j\text{ with }(u,v)\in E\text{ and revising }u\text{ invalidates }v\}\). The repair cascade is the fixed-point set \(S_\infty=\bigcup_{j\geq0}S_j\); its depth is the largest finite propagation index and its size is \(|S_\infty|\). A containment boundary \(B\subseteq V\) succeeds when \(S_\infty\subseteq B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repair cascade is the transitive set of commitments invalidated by an initial change; its size, depth, and containment boundary quantify propagation.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) records decision-relevant invalidation dependencies.
Cascade propagation is evaluated until a fixed point is reached.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_\infty\) is the least dependency-closed set containing the directly repaired commitments.

notation.meaning: Commitments changed directly by the initial repair.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-point cascade concept matches the leaf, but the stated depth as the 'largest finite propagation index' is not well defined because the sequence remains equal to its fixed point at every later index. It should instead use the least stabilization index or longest strict propagation chain, supported by a source.

children.title: Operational Instability
children.top_down_role: Repeated or disruptive changes that undermine execution stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Operational Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily small disruptions force nonvanishing changes in feasible integrated operating decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a metric space of disruptions and \(S(u)\subseteq X\) the nonempty set of feasible integrated decisions under disruption \(u\). With decision metric \(d_X\), the system is operationally stable at \(u_0\) if there exist \(K,\delta>0\) such that every \(u\) with \(d_U(u,u_0)<\delta\) admits \(x\in S(u)\) and \(x_0\in S(u_0)\) satisfying \(d_X(x,x_0)\leq Kd_U(u,u_0)\). Operational instability holds when this local bounded-response condition fails; in particular, arbitrarily small disruptions may require a decision change bounded below by a fixed positive amount.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Operational instability occurs when arbitrarily small disruptions can force substantial changes in every feasible integrated plan, schedule, or configuration.
assumptions_latex: Feasible decision sets are nonempty near the reference disruption.
Metrics quantify disruption magnitude and integrated decision change.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of the stated local bounded-response condition defines operational instability at \(u_0\).

notation.meaning: Feasible integrated decisions under disruption u.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact stability notion is not source-backed, and failure of the stated existential Lipschitz selection condition does not imply that every feasible response undergoes a change bounded below by a fixed positive amount. The plain statement therefore overstates the LaTeX condition. An authoritative choice among calmness, Lipschitz selection, and set-valued stability notions is needed.

children.title: Cross-Domain Change Propagation
children.top_down_role: Transmission of revised decisions across planning, scheduling, and configuration boundaries.

assumptions_latex: The integrated constraint model has finite variable blocks \(V=P\mathbin{\dot\cup}S\mathbin{\dot\cup}C\) for planning, scheduling, and configuration.
Each propagator \(g\in\mathcal G\) has a finite read set \(R_g\subseteq V\) and write set \(W_g\subseteq V\).
Propagation is iterated to a least fixed point after an initial changed set \(U\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A variable in a domain block distinct from every block meeting \(U\) is cross-domain affected exactly when it belongs to \(\operatorname{Prop}(U)\).

notation.meaning: Planning, scheduling, and configuration variable blocks.
Propagation closure of the initially changed variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite fixed-point model of propagation among planning, scheduling, and configuration variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\subseteq V\), define \(T(X)=X\cup igcup\{W_g:g\in\mathcal G,\ R_g\cap X
eq\varnothing\}\) and \(\operatorname{Prop}(U)= igcup_{k\geq 0}T^k(U)\). Cross-domain change propagation occurs from block \(D_i\in\{P,S,C\}\) to a distinct block \(D_j\) when \(U\cap D_i
eq\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{Prop}(U)\cap D_j
eq\varnothing\). Its block-level reach is \(ho(U)=|\{D\in\{P,S,C\}:D\cap\operatorname{Prop}(U)
eq\varnothing\}|\). Thus propagation is genuinely cross-domain precisely when \(ho(U)\) exceeds the number of domain blocks intersecting \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-domain propagation is the least fixed-point closure of an initial change that reaches a planning, scheduling, or configuration block not initially changed.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Domain Change Propagation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite propagation-closure definition is internally coherent and the definition kind fits the leaf, but no citation supports this particular read-set/write-set formalization or its interpretation for coupled planning, scheduling, and configuration. Source support is required before its mathematical version can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Commitment Churn
children.top_down_role: Repeated replacement of previously accepted operational commitments.

assumptions_latex: Repairs produce a sequence of integrated assignments \(x^0,x^1,\ldots,x^T\).
A designated set \(K\subseteq V\) contains variables whose assigned values constitute operational commitments.
Weights \(w_v>0\) encode the cost or importance of revising commitment \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Commitment churn is absent exactly when \(x_v^t=x_v^{t-1}\) for every \(v\in K\) and every \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\).

notation.meaning: Commitment variables across the coupled model.
Integrated assignment after repair step t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted revision count for commitments during finite integrated repair sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The weighted commitment churn of the repair sequence is \[\operatorname{Churn}_K(x^{0:T})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{v\in K}w_v\,\mathbf 1\!\left[x_v^t\neq x_v^{t-1}\right].\] The distinct-commitment churn is \(\operatorname{DChurn}_K(x^{0:T})=|\{v\in K:\exists t\in\{1,\ldots,T\},\ x_v^t\neq x_v^{t-1}\}|\). The first quantity counts repeated reversals separately, whereas the second counts each revised commitment once. For a budget \(B\geq0\), the sequence has bounded churn when \(\operatorname{Churn}_K(x^{0:T})\leq B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Commitment churn measures weighted changes to designated committed variables across successive repairs, counting either every revision or each revised commitment once.
knowledge_statements.title: Commitment Churn

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two churn measures are well-defined and the definition kind fits the leaf, but no source establishes that weighted transition counts and distinct revised-variable counts represent commitment churn in integrated repair sequences. A domain-specific citation with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Cascade Containment Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting how far local repair effects propagate.

assumptions_latex: The directed dependency graph is \(G=(V,E)\), with an arc \((u,v)\in E\) when a change at \(u\) can require reconsidering \(v\).
The initial changed set is \(U\subseteq V\), and \(Q\subseteq V\) is the protected region.
A proposed boundary \(B\subseteq V\setminus(U\cup Q)\) can be fixed or revalidated independently of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(B\) certifies containment precisely when it separates \(U\) from \(Q\); after removing \(B\), no propagation path from \(U\) reaches \(Q\).

notation.meaning: Initial changed and protected variable sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-separator certificate for containing change cascades before they reach protected variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(B\) is a cascade-containment boundary between \(U\) and \(Q\) if every directed path in \(G\) beginning in \(U\) and ending in \(Q\) contains a vertex of \(B\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{Reach}_{G-B}(U)\cap Q=\varnothing\). A verifiable certificate consists of \(B\) and the reachable set \(R=\operatorname{Reach}_{G-B}(U)\): verification checks \(U\subseteq R\), \(R\cap Q=\varnothing\), and that no arc \((r,v)\in E\) satisfies \(r\in R\) and \(v\notin R\cup B\). Under the dependency-graph semantics, these checks certify that any propagated cascade from \(U\) must encounter \(B\) before reaching \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A containment boundary is a verifiable vertex separator that every dependency path from an initial change to protected variables must cross.
knowledge_statements.title: Cascade Containment Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vertex-separator certificate and reachable-set checks are mathematically coherent, and the certificate kind is appropriate because the record supplies verifiable containment evidence. However, no cited source supports the dependency-graph semantics or its application as a cascade-containment boundary in this domain.
